THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Cootie Williams

Washington, D. C.
May 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
Okay. We're now talking to Cootie Williams. And this is Helen Oakley doing the -- Helen Oakley Dance, doing the interview.
Cootie, let's start right at the beginning, and supposing you tell me what year you were born.
Well, I was born July the 10th, 1911, in Mobile, Alabama.
And will you tell me about your family? About your mother and father and how many children there were in the family and so on.

There was four boys and we all had to take music. My mother played the organ in church, and the piano, and so we all had to take music. And I was the only one that followed her footsteps, I would say. The rest of them went into other fields.
Well, which son were you? Were you number one, two, or what?
I was number three.
You were number three. How many years difference were there between you and your brothers?
Well, the oldest one was seven years older than me. The other one was three years older than me.
I see. Was it your father or your mother who insisted on you studying music? It was your mother, wasn't
Yeah.
And what -- did they all -- did everybody study piano then?
Yeah. A little bit. I was a drummer.
You were a drummer.
I loved the drums.
So you had a feeling for the drums right away, did you?
Uh-huh.
And did your father buy you some drums then?
Yes.
Well, how old were you then?
I think maybe around about five.
Oh, that's wonderful.
About five or six years old.
Well, let's go back a minute. Other than your mother, was there music in your family farther back? Your grandmother or grandfather?
I don't remember them.
You don't.
No music, no. Only my mother.
Only your mother. And she was an organist as well.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
At church. And how old were you when your mother died, then?
I think I was about seven years old. Seven or eight years old.
I think you told me before that your mother gave birth to twins.
Yes.
And that was the occasion of her death?
Yeah. One of them died and one of them lived.
One of them lived. Well, the twin that lived, was that the fourth brother?
Yeah. That was the fourth brother.
That was the fourth brother. There were no sisters?
No sisters.
Oh, I see. Well, then, how did your father manage, then? With a baby and three other boys to take care of. What happened at home?
Well, my aunt sort of raised us.
I see. I see. And, well, what did your father do in Mobile, Cootie?
Well, he did sort of a lot of different things. First he worked for a furrier. He used to go to the
What kind of furs?
Whatever they killed.
I mean, what would there be there? Muskrat or would there be mink, or --
I don't recall.
You don't recall.
Right now. But I know that's what he did.
I suppose people on the farms trapped them or something.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And he used to go out in the country and buy these furs from these people.
I see.
Give them little or nothing for them.
Yes.
(Laughter)
And eventually he and another fellow opened up a gambling place there in Mobile.
Tell me about that. What was it like?
Well --
I mean, was it on the main street?
Yes, it was on the main street.
I see.
Davis Avenue.
Yeah.
We called it the Street there. And -- of course, I wasn't allowed in there.
No.
I didn't ever get to look at it. I knew where it was situated, but he didn't allow me in the pool room.
There was a pool room?
No. It wasn't -- he didn't own the pool room.
Oh.
But he didn't allow me to go into the pool room.
No. No. Well, Cootie, what did they do, shoot craps and --
I don't know what all they did.
-- play blackjack. You don't know.
I don't know what he had in the gambling place.
But he did all right.
Oh, yeah.
I mean he did this for a long time?
Yeah. He was very successful at it.
Oh, well that was good, then. So you come by it legitimately, Cootie.
(Laughter)
And then he started going to New Orleans, to the race track.
Oh, so that's what I'm talking about when I say legitimately.
Yeah.
I see. So, how far would New Orleans be from Mobile?
90 miles.
90 miles. What would he do, drive?
Yeah. Or catch the train and go over there.
Yeah. And go down for the races.
Yeah. And that's how he got broke.
Oh. How many years did that go on?

That didn't go on many years, I don't think, because when I came to New York, it was '28, 1928. He wrote me a letter and told me he was going to sell the house, the home, if I didn't come home. So I wrote back and told him to sell it, because I wasn't coming back home. So he lost the home, lost the gambling place, lost everything.
Oh, Cootie. And he did all right with the gambling place, and it was on the horses that he lost
everything.
Yeah.
Well, why did he ask you if you were coming home? Wasn't your younger brother at home?
Yeah.
And what about the other two boys?
No.
They had moved out?
They had moved out.
I see. So he meant just for himself and the younger boy, unless you were going to come and be earning money, I guess.
Maybe so.
Well, what a shame. What did he do then? What happened?
Well, he left Mobile then, I think, and he went to Houston, Texas. Then he was a sort of a strike breaker. When the men would go on strike, he would bring in other men to work.
Oh, I see. Well, wasn't that a little dangerous?
Yeah. It was dangerous. He got shot.
He did?
Yeah.
Tell me about it. First of all, was he a
big man --
Yeah.
-- small man?
A real big man. A strong man. They wanted to train him to fight Jack Johnson.
Really?
(Laughter)
For heaven's sake.
Real tall, strong man. Oh, but he wouldn't do that. So after he got shot in Houston --
There was the strikers, huh?
Yeah. Some kind of way. I wasn't --
I was in New York then.
Yeah.
So I went down there to see him.
Oh, you did.
Yeah.
What year was that? I mean I'm interested because I just wondered when did you leave New York and go down and see him? Can you remember?
I can't remember the exact year.
I mean, it wasn't when you were with Duke, was it?
Yeah. Yeah.
Oh, it was.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
And so you went down and saw him. Was he in hospital?
Yeah.
Oh, dear. Was he badly off?
Yeah. But he pulled through that.
Oh. And then what happened? No more strike breaking, I hope.
No. Then he turned in to be a minister.
Did he?
Yeah.
Did he really?
(Laughter)
For goodness sake. When did he find the church?
I don't know. He came to New York after he got well. Then he came to live with me. But he didn't want me to drink, didn't want me to have no company. I had a big bar in the basement of my home.
Were you married?
Yeah.
You and Catherine were married then.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
And he didn't want you to drink?
He didn't want me to have no company that drank or drink alcohol. And --
What a funny thing.
And I told him no. I said, "No, Dad, that wouldn't work." Not with my friends and my wife's friends. So he went and stayed with my younger brother. My youngest brother was here then.
Oh. What was he doing?
He was working at some club downtown. Just working as a layman.
Yeah.

That's what he was doing. So he stayed with him for a pretty good while. I told him that I would give him the money to stay anyplace else he wanted to stay. So he got mad with me. Because I wouldn't give up the things, you know.
Yeah.
In the early days, of course, I used to like to drink and used to have parties and entertain.
But wasn't he proud of you, of being a, you know, a well known musician in a very well known band? Wasn't he impressed with that?
Oh, yeah.
He was proud of that, but he wanted you to live differently.
But I had my own band then.
Oh, it was then. It was way up in --
Yeah, I had my own band.
In the '50s, then. Or something.
Yeah. Maybe in the '40s.
Oh. Yeah.
In the late '40s.
Yeah. Late '40s. Right. Oh, I see. Well, of -- oh, I see. Cootie, you had told me you had started to drink a little bit heavily then, you told me before. Am I right?
Yes, uh-huh.
Well, we don't want to jump that far ahead, but maybe this was what he had on his mind, was it?
No. Well, as I knew my dad, he was a good time man.
He was a what?
He was a good time type of person, you know?
Oh, yes. Right. Right.
And this was a new person coming to me.
Yes.
And I couldn't understand it.
No. Of course not.
And I provided a place for him, when I bought my home on Long Island, out there. So this time, when he came to me with all of this, different things, he shocked me.
Yeah. Of course.
So he stayed in New York for a pretty good while.
Had he had a real change of heart, Cootie, or was he getting older and he thought differently then, or what was it?
Well, Helen, I don't know. My father was the type of man -- his was to get a dollar.
Yeah.
You know. He was going to get that dollar from some kind of way.
Yeah.
And maybe if he couldn't come through me he was coming through somebody.
Yeah.
He was going to get that dollar.
Yeah.
So, he decided he wanted to go to California. So he didn't want to see me, so he sent my younger
brother out to the house to tell me that he wanted to go to California, he needed some money. So I think I sent him $300.00.
So he was mad with you, he wouldn't talk with you, but he wanted the money.
Oh, yeah. But he got the money. If there was anything I wanted while I was coming up, when he had money he gave it to me.
Yeah.
So I wouldn't deny him of anything, you know.
No.
You know, what I had.
Yeah.
And I gave him $300.00. And that's about the last -- that's about the last I heard of him.
Is it really?
Until he passed away.
When did he pass away?
Oh, this was in the '50s.
Oh. Was he -- none of the boys were there? He didn't --
No.
That was sad, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Well, you felt good that you'd helped him to get out there.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
Oh, yeah.
Cootie, let's just see what we've got here a minute.
Okay. We're recording. Right, Cootie. How about your mother?
Well, my mother, she was a religious type of woman.
Who did you favor? Who did you look like?
Well, I was in between her and my father.
Were you? Yeah.
Yeah.
And who were you -- I mean, the four boys, were some of you like your father in character, or like your mother, or what? What about yourself?
Well, I was between both of them.
And for character too, huh?
Yeah. Character too. My mother and my father.
Yeah. Why, what was your mother like?
She was religious.
Yeah. And she played music. And --
Was she a disciplinarian, or not too much, huh?
Not too much, no.
No. She was kind hearted?
Yeah.
Yeah.
I never did get a whupping from her.
You never got a whupping?
No. Not from her.
That right. That's wonderful, isn't it?
Yeah.
Yeah. You did from your dad, though?
Oh, yeah.
(Laughter)
Not too much --
No.
-- because I was afraid of my father.
Oh, you were.
Yeah.
Why? Was he that strict or that removed from you, or what?
Yeah. In a way. I was about the only
one afraid of him.
You were?
Yeah.
Why weren't the others?
They didn't mind getting those whuppings.
Oh.
And I did.
I see.
(Laughter)
They just took it in their stride, huh?
Yeah.
So you would be a little careful not to do things that would bring it on, huh?
That's right.
Yeah.
He used to whip my youngest brother and I used to cry. But --
When he whipped your youngest brother, you used to cry?
Yeah.
Oh.
And about the next hour, he'd be doing the same thing over again.
Oh. So he didn't really care.
No.
Fancy that. Which of the brothers were you close with? Any of them?
Yes.
The little one?
Yeah, the little one. And the one next to me. The one was three years older than me.
Yeah.
The other, oldest one, he was gone all the time.
He was that much older than you.
Yeah.
Yeah.
He helped to raise us too.
Did he?
Yeah.
That was nice.
The oldest one did.
Yeah. Oh, the oldest one did?
Yeah.
Oh, you mean he helped to bring home some money, too, you mean? Or just to look out for you.
Look out for us.
Yeah. Well, that was good.
After my mother passed.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, your mother and dad, they got along nicely together? Or did she have a little bit of a hard time with your father?
No. She had a hard time with him.
Yeah.
He told me that.
Yeah.
He said he was gone all the time.
Yeah. And if he was a gambling man --
Yeah.
-- I guess -- well, at least she didn't have to see when he blew everything.
No. She wasn't living then.
No. Did she have a big family, Cootie? Was it her sister who came?
Yeah.
Oh.
It was a big family, yeah. A real big family.
All from Mobile?
No. They were all from Alabama.
Oh.
A little town up there. What was it? I don't recall.
You don't remember?
No.
Tell me what you do -- tell me about Mobile in those days, what it was like. It was kind of wide open, wasn't it? Wasn't there plenty of life, plenty going on?
Yes, it was.
Because I guess, being a seaport.
Yeah. Being a seaport town.
Was it a little more open?
Yeah.
A little less narrow?
It was sort of a wide open town.
Yeah.
And --
Were there a lot of, what, speakeasies and -- or was that not that far back, I guess, huh?
No.
Prohibition was, what, in the early '30s?
Yeah.
And that was before that.
That was before that. Well, I know they used to have a red light district. And I used to deliver papers. I was a paper boy.
Yeah.
And I remember that.
Yeah.
And --
But there was no traffic in dope or anything like that?
No.
In those days there wasn't, really, was there? That much.
No. No.
I guess maybe there was in New York. I don't know.
No, no.
Not down there.
I didn't know nothing about things like that.
Well, what about -- I'll tell you one thing that Trummy (PHONETIC) told us, was that blues singers used to come in from the country. And used to -- you know, play guitar, country blues singers.
Yeah. Country blues singers.
Do you remember that at all?
I don't remember any blues singers like that.
No? Do you remember any little bands?
No. The only bands I remember was the brass band, the Excelsior Brass Band, which my teacher was
playing in.
Was that the teacher --
Charlie Lipscomb.
Yeah. He's the one that wouldn't let you play any jazz.
Yeah. He was the one that wouldn't let me play any jazz.
Well, tell us. You might just as well tell us about that, because you studied with him a long time, didn't you?
Yes.
You got a terrific foundation from him.
Yes, I did.
Well, first of all, how was it you switched from drums?
Well, we was in the school band.
What school was it? Can you remember?
That would be an elementary school.
Yeah. And during rehearsals, everybody went out to play. And I picked up the trumpet and started to playing "Twelfth Street Rag".
Well, how could you?
I don't know.
Well, you'd heard "Twelfth Street Rag", had you?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And I had a knack of going around and picking up all the instruments at the time, you know.
Oh, yeah.
And I picked up this trumpet and started to play "Twelfth Street Rag".
So were you using the valves?

Yeah. And the bandmaster heard this thing, and he come running in there, and said, "That's the instrument for you." I said, "Oh, no. Oh, no. Oh, no. I'm a drummer. I ain't playing that." And so that's how I started playing the trumpet. I got a whipping and he made me play the trumpet.
You got a whipping? From who?
From the bandmaster.
No. He really argued with you about it? I see. Well, he must have had a sharp ear, then. He could hear --
Yeah. He was a trumpet player.
Oh, he was a trumpet player.
Yeah.
Oh, I see. Isn't that funny, though, that you still preferred playing the drums.
I still preferred playing the drums.
Isn't that funny?
And so that's how I started playing the trumpet. So after --
How old were you then?
I was quite young.
About nine?
Maybe -- nine, maybe.
Yeah.
Eight or nine years old.
Yeah.
So after that, they turned me over to -- my father and Charlie Lipscomb were good friends.
Oh. Uh-huh.
So he put me in Charlie Lipscomb's hands.
Yeah. What did -- Charlie Lipscomb was in the Excelsior Band.
Yeah.
Was that what he did for a livelihood?
Well, he had a pressing club. A cleaning and pressing club.
Oh, yeah.
Then, after school, I would go there and deliver clothes on the bicycle. And I worked for him. He gave me $4.00 a week and my lesson.
And your lesson.
Yeah. He wouldn't --
Well, that was pretty good money for a kid in those days, wasn't it, you know?
Yeah. That was good money.
That'd get you quite a lot of stuff.
Yeah. That was good money. And during business was slow, at the time, he would teach me.
Oh, I see. Yeah. Nothing doing, and he'd tell you to get your horn out.

Yeah. So if he would give me a lesson to take home to learn, I would be listening to jazz records, Louis Armstrong records, trying to copy them, and wouldn't pay the lesson no mind. And when I'd come back for him to go over the lesson with me -- when he got ready to go over the lesson with me, I wouldn't know none of it. And by the time he started hitting me on my head --
What with?
With his hand. Anything he had.
Yeah.

I got sick and tired of him bopping me on my head. I said, 'Louis Armstrong and everybody else is going to have to go. I'm going to get this lesson.' And so I would begin to get the lesson. And that's when I started.
Well, what kind of a music book did he
have you on?
(Arban)
He had me on the album. I think that was -- yeah, album.
Oh, yeah. Right. And so you were doing exercises out of that.
Yeah.
Was he -- could he move around on the horn himself?
Oh, yeah. He was a terrific trumpeter.
He was?
Yeah.
He really was?
Uh-huh.
Oh. Strong?
Yeah.
And a good tone?
Yeah.
Oh. Well, you were fortunate weren't you?
Oh, yeah.
And he had a good embouchure.
Yeah.
So you didn't have any embouchure trouble right from the start then?
No.
I mean, he didn't have to tell you anything about blowing. You just -- it came naturally, how to blow.
Yeah. It came naturally how to blow.
He taught you about breathing.
Yeah. He taught me about breathing.
Well. You studied with him about eight years, didn't you?
I studied with him for quite a while.
Well, so what, would he work you through that book --
Yeah.
-- and take you onto the next book, and so on?
Yeah.
But all that time, he was determined you wouldn't play jazz?
That's right.
Did he think you didn't? Did he think you were doing what you were told?
(Laughter)
Or did he not care to think about it?
Well, just as long as I came in with those lessons.
Yeah. He didn't --
He didn't bother about what I was doing.
Yeah.
In the beginning, I started to messing up. Then he straightened me out.
Yeah. But once he had you doing his work --
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, Cootie, so it was in this working out these exercises and everything all the time, that you began to really develop the habit of reading, then.
Oh, yeah.
So, I mean, that just all came as a part of blowing. The reading was another part of blowing.
Yeah.
Which it wasn't in a lot of people's cases, was it? You know, a lot of people found out how to blow one way or another, and they weren't actually reading at the same time, were they?
That's right.
I mean, a lot of people didn't work from books at all, did they?
I'll tell you. By him doing that, I got a break. I got one of the biggest breaks in my life. That's how I became known, by him making me do that. I come to New

York and I -- Pop Smith was with Fletcher Henderson and he quit. [He up to bad.] So someone told Fletcher about me. I was working with Chick Webb then, but Chick wasn't working. So he came by and asked Chick could I go to work with him. And Chick said, 'Yeah, I'll let you have him to go out on this trip.' So I went with Fletcher. No rehearsal or nothing. Playing first trumpet.
First trumpet. In that band. That was really a tall order, wasn't it?

It sure was. So if I hadn't been schooled properly, I never would have made it. No rehearsal or nothing. First job, put the music in front of me, and I just played it just like it was, you know, A, B, C.

Well, Cootie, you must have -- I mean there's a question of the way that band phrased and everything. You at least were familiar with the sound of that band, weren't you? You were familiar with it, weren't you? You had heard the band.
Yeah. His music was marked. The phrasing -- all the phrasing was marked through there. And so I went and played it --
Like it was there.
Just like it was. You know, by being under my teacher, and he made me phrase and do the things -- the marking of the music.
Yeah. Yeah.
And that paid off.
Yeah. That's wonderful. That really is. Well, listen, we won't -- that's another period that we'll be coming to.
Yeah.
So we won't go into that.
Okay.

We'll go back. Well, one thing though, like -- as you were studying like seven or eight years with him, what did he have you doing? Did he have you playing trumpet parts or big parts? I mean, how did he keep bringing you on all the time?
Well, sometimes me and him would play duets.
Oh, you would.
Yeah. Duets.
That was good. Yeah.
We played duets.

Oh, that was good. Well then I'm bringing it up to -- because I know that you went to the carnival. Your father took you and you heard Lester and Lee Young's father's band and everything. And I know you went there. But just before we talk about that, didn't you -- well, first of all, did you have a phonograph in the house?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Your father had got a phonograph.
Yeah.
Well, did your brothers like to listen to Louis Armstrong? and so on? Did other people get those records?
Well, no. They wasn't particular about music. During that era. They had give it up.
Well, where did you get the records? Did you buy them?
Yeah, I would get them or my father would get them.
Oh. Well, did your father like that music?
Yeah.
Oh, he did.
Yeah, my father liked that music.
And then you'd get the records, too.
Yeah.
Who else did you listen to? You listened to Louis. Did you listen to Bessie?
No. I didn't listen to singers.
You didn't.
I was only interested in trumpets.
Is that right? Well, did you -- did you listen to King Oliver, then?
Yes. I listened to him, but not on records. I listened to King Oliver in later years on records, but during that period of time, I only listened to Louis.
Is that right.
Yeah.
Is that so. Was Earl on those records? Was it those records? "Monday Date" and those early ones?
I think his wife was playing the piano on them.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I see. Lil.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. So that was when he was in Chicago, in those early days.
Yeah.
Yeah. Oh, so you knew those records backwards, don't you, Cootie?
Yeah.
Did you blow them? Did you get it down?
Yeah.
You blew it.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. Well, what did you -- did you feel a terrific excitement? I know you must have, because you've been absolutely wrapped up in music all your life. I want you to tell me how it felt when you first found you were -- well,
what was your -- what did you feel when you first heard those Louis records? You must have had a big feeling, didn't you?
Yes.
Did you run a temperature or something?
Yes. I thought he was the greatest thing I ever heard.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah. You mean that beat.
Yeah. And that sound.
And that sound.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, I guess that you knew right then that was going to be it for you always, huh?
Yeah.
Did you?
Yeah.
It didn't grow on you. You did know it for sure?
Yeah. Well, nearly everyone had an idol. And he was my idol.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, didn't you -- weren't you hopeful of getting together with some kid that played some piano, or -- I mean, weren't you anxious to try to hear yourself, or didn't you know anybody that played any piano of that kind of
Well, yes. Before I left home, the bands from New Orleans used to come over there and play dances. So they used to balley-hoo, and --
What do you mean? Come outside and --
Yeah. They used to be on a truck.
Oh, yes.
And go around and stop at different streets and play.
Yeah.
And advertise the dance.
In the daytime?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And sometimes I used to play with them.
You standing on the street?
Yeah. Sometimes they'd let me play with them.
Would they let you get up on the truck?
Yeah.
No kidding.
After they knew about me, they let me play with them.
Well, I'll be darned.
And so --
So that way you began to get to know the numbers.
Yeah. The numbers and things.
Yeah.
So Edmund Hall Hogg was playing with the Pensacola Jazz Band, and they came to Mobile, and I sat in with them and played. And that's how I got started out.
Well, tell me something about that band. First of all, how old was Edmund Hall Hogg when he was playing in that band? A little older than you?
Oh, yeah. He was older than me, yeah.
Was he?
Yeah. I was a kid then. A teenager, maybe. I was maybe about 16 years old, I think.
Yeah. And he was like 20 or something like that, huh?
I think he was a little older than that.
Was he?
Yeah.
Well, who all was in that band?
I can't remember.
Well, what was it? I mean, was it clarinet, trumpet and trombone and rhythm?
Yeah.
That's what the band was?
Yeah. A regular Dixieland style band.
Yeah. So you don't remember who the trumpet player was that you replaced, then, huh?
No. I didn't replace nobody. I didn't go with the band.
Oh. You didn't go with the band?
No.
Oh.
I just would sit in with them while they were there.
Oh, I see. Oh, yeah. That was good. Well, so that means that you were getting all that by ear.
Yeah.
A lot of that wasn't even written.
No, no. They didn't have no music.
No.
They played by ear. They didn't have no music. And Edmund Hall left the Pensacola Jazz Band, and he went to Florida to join another band by the name of Eagle Eye Shields.
Was that a bandleader?
Yeah.
What did he play?
He played piano.
Yeah.

And he told him about me. So they got in touch with my father. My father's partner in the gambling house business happened to live in Jacksonville, Florida. So he told them he would have to talk to his partner about it first. To see if the partner would take care of me. So the partner said yes, that he would look after me. And so that's how I got a chance to leave home. To go down there to play with Eagle Eye Shields. His was the first band I ever played with.
Well, was Eagle Eye Shields working in Jacksonville?
Yeah.
Oh. Well listen, I want to understand something. If this was your father's partner, you mean he put up half the money with your father?
Yeah.
He put up -- so he wasn't in Mobile, but he put up -- he put up --
He was a gambler.
Yeah. I see. So he'd move around, you mean.
Yeah.
And he put up money, along with your father, and they owned the place together.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I see. But did he have a place of his own in Jacksonville, too?
No.
A gambling place?
No. He gambled with the biggest gamblers in America.
He did?
This man in Jacksonville. And how he did it was he looked like a white man.
Oh, I see.
And he used to pass for white.
I see. So he'd get in on big games.
Yeah.
Is that right? What, in gambling houses?
No.
What, then?
With all the big gamblers and big games that was going on in America then. Wherever they would have these big games, he would go and gamble with them.
Yeah.
And they found out that he was a Negro. And they killed him.
Oh, my God. Is that -- there in Jacksonville?
Uh-huh.
They lost money to him and they found out.
He was the smartest gambler of all of them.
Would you believe. Good God. When? Not when you were living there?
Yeah. It happened during the time I was there.
Cootie.
I think he was sitting on the front porch.
And what happened?
They just blowed him away.
With a gun, you mean?
Yeah.
My God. Isn't that awful. Didn't he -- well, I suppose he was a gambler, but he might have thought that -- he must have known it was a risky thing. Or did he think they'd never find out?

Well, a gambler like him, I don't know what would run what he -- it wouldn't cross his mind, because things like that didn't come across my mind, because the only thing I'd be thinking about would be music.
Yeah. And he had a family, Cootie?
No. He didn't have any kids, no.
But he was taking care of you.
Yeah. And his wife.
Oh. Oh. Well, that's a sad thing, isn't it?
Yeah.
Those games, did they take place in people's houses, I guess, huh?
No. He gambled with the biggest gamblers in America.
Well, where would they gamble?
Well, I don't know.
Yeah.
I'm only going by what my father told me, you know.
Yeah. Well, that's a horrible thing, isn't it?
Yeah.
Well, so -- well, what happened. By that time, I mean, your father, he said you could live there under his care and be in the band.
Uh-huh.
By that time you'd been in the band a little time, I guess.
Yeah.
Maybe you were 17 or 18 then.
Yeah. Then I stayed with the band, with Eagle Eye, for quite awhile. I don't know exactly how many years. Then I went with Alonzo Ross's band. He was from Florida, too.
Yeah.
Edmund Hall went.
Yeah.
And I went with Edmund Hall.

Yeah. Cootie, before I -- it's a shame to interrupt you, but before we get too far away from it, I want you to recall back, when you went to that carnival, because that's very interesting. You worked that summer with Lester and Lee and their father.
Yeah. That was in --
How old were you then?
I imagine I was around ten or twelve years old.
Oh. As little as that?
Yeah.
And your father took you to the carnival?
Yeah.
Any of the others of you, or just you?
Me and maybe my other brother.
Yeah.
I can't recall. Just me because I
loved music.
Well, that's why he took you.
Yeah. So I heard Lester playing.
No kidding.
And I said, 'Dad, I sure do want to play with them.' And he was talking, and so on the way back home, he says, -- wait a minute, now -- the next day, I think, I went around and played with them.
You did?
Yeah. I had my horn and went around and played with them.
What did you do? I mean, tell me about it. What was it like? Were they -- was it a tent?
Yeah. It was a tent.
And you went around in the daytime?
I went around in the daytime. He talked to Lester's father. He had the band.
Yeah. He was a trumpet player, wasn't he?
No. Saxophone player.
Oh.
All of them were saxophone players. There was Lester, Lee and ISMA Heerman.
Well, didn't Lee play drums?
Not during that time. He played
saxophone, too. Oh.
The whole family played saxophone.
Oh.
And the stepmother.
Oh.
So they had an act on the stage.
Like five saxophones.
Yeah. With the family.
Yeah.
Playing saxophones. And my father talked with him. He wanted me, after he heard me play.
He did.
Yeah. So my father said, 'Well, I can't let him go away from home by himself, because he's too young. You'll have to take his older brother.' The one older to me, next to me.
The one next to you.
So he said, 'Yeah, I'll take him.'
What did he have him do?
Nothing. He didn't do nothing. He worked on the carnival, doing different things.
Is that right? Yeah.
And that's how I went on the show with Lester.
So that was the first time you were ever before the public.
Yeah.
Was that a scary feeling?
No.
Didn't it ever bother you?
My teacher stopped me from being scared.
How?

By -- if I'd get nervous like that, he'd hit me and say, 'Don't you ever get nervous doing nothing in music. Because you can't produce when you get nervous.' And he'd hit me like that. 'Don't you never.'
Is that right?
Yeah. And he broke me out of that habit of being nervous.
Well, that was a marvelous thing to have done for you, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Most everybody suffers from nerves, don't they?
Yeah. And I never did be nervous, throughout my career.
Is that right.
Yeah. I never was nervous.

Well, I'll be darned. Well, Cootie, go back to him. There's a couple of things I wanted to ask you about it. You know, Lester said, you know, that he was frightened of his father, that his father was rough on them, was hard on them, and that, in fact -- I don't know -- I saw where Lester said one time that he'd blown, and his father didn't like what he blew, and he bawled him out. And I think he bawled him out in front of people. Made him feel very bad, and said he never -- he was against his father from then on. Well, did you -- of course you were pretty young, but was he a hard man? Mr. Young?
Well, I don't think so. I don't think so, in a way of speaking. Lester wanted to leave. He had plenty of offers during the period of time I was there, to go with white bands.
Is that right?
Yeah.
What white band?
I done forgot the band.
One particular band, you mean?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And his father wouldn't let him go.
He wasn't going to pass, was he?
Yeah.
Oh, I see. And so he -- that made him
feel bad.
Yeah.
I see. Well, was he -- was he blowing so much then?
Yeah.
He was.
Uh-huh.
But was it different? It wasn't like Hawk. Or was it?
No, no. It wasn't like no Hawk.
Even then it wasn't?
No.
He still had that tone?
Yeah.
And he still had that different concept, huh?
Yeah.
So he really was an innovator with that concept, wasn't he?
Yeah. That's what made me wanted to go with them.
Is that right?
Because he was different from anybody I ever heard.
Is that right? That's very funny, because
in a way, the style that -- well, I mean the style -- your idol was Louis.
Yeah.
And Lester was playing a style that was coming after the style that Louis established. Am I right in thinking that?
Well, yeah. He was a stylist.
Yeah.
And he was the next person I'd ever heard in person.
Yeah.
He was the greatest thing I'd ever heard in person.
Yeah. Right. Yeah. He was the biggest talent you'd come across personally.
Yeah. In person.
Yeah. Cause he had a different feel for the beat, didn't he.
Yeah.
It was a different feel.
Yeah. And I wanted to learn something about it.
No kidding?
Uh-huh.
And did you pick up that feel?
Yeah, I learned something from him.
You did?
Yeah.
Well, like what?
In the beat, in different syncopations that he had.
Is that right?
Uh-huh.
Did -- well, he was what, like five years older than you?
I imagine so, yeah.
Was he nice with you?
Oh, yeah, he was nice. But during that time, I couldn't hang out with him. And I would be with Lee and Irma.
Why? Because you were that much younger?
Yeah. And the father.
Yeah.
The father never did give me no money. He was supposed to send my father the money.
He didn't?
No. Sometimes he'd give me 50 cents. Sometimes.
Oh, my.
But he'd feed me. We'd go to dinner.
(Laughter)
I didn't pay it any mind. I was happy.
Yeah. You were getting what you came for.
Yeah.
Well, Cootie, Lester must have recognized that you could blow.
Maybe so. Maybe so.
But he always did live in kind of a world of his own, didn't he?
Yeah. Sort of quietly by himself.
Yeah. Not coming out into the.-- so he was always himself, right then and there. Yeah. Yeah. I see. How long did you stay? Was it during one summer?

Yeah. It was during one summer. We got ready to come home, and our father sent us some money so we could come home, me and my brother. So my father sent us this money to come home, and my brother bought me a ticket and put me on the train, and he hoboed.
(Laughter)
Was that what he wanted to do?
Yeah. He -- (Laughter).
Was your father mad?
No, my father wasn't mad, because he knew him. He was --
That's how he was, huh?
Yeah, that's how he was.
That was quite nervy of him, wasn't it? What, was he only 15?
No, he was older than that.
Oh, was he?
Yeah.
Oh, he was.
He might be around 17.
Oh, yeah.
But he was wild, you know.
Yeah. So he put you on a train.
Yeah. He put me on the train and he hoboed.
Where were you? Do you know?
I don't remember, right off.
Did you go -- during that summer, did you go to big towns?
Yeah.
Oh, you did?
Uh-huh.
Did you go to New Orleans?
The only place I can remember, a big town, was East St. Louis.
Oh, you did go there?
Yeah.
Fancy that.
Because I bought me a suit there.
Did you?

And the day I bought the suit, I worked in the carnival. They would be tearing it down. I would go and help them tear down the ferris wheel. I saved up that money. So when we got to East St. Louis, I went to a pawn shop and bought me a long pants suit.
You didn't.
I got me this suit. Yeah.
That was your first long pants?
Yeah.
No kidding. And then you started to wear it, right?
Yeah.

How about that. That's funny, isn't it? Well, listen. If you were blowing with them for about three months, that's one time when you came to know the library, because they must have played everything that was -- all the standards and everything, huh?
Yeah.
What other kinds of things did they play? I mean, they didn't play march music or anything did they?
No. Well, I tell you, we played for the people in the show. They had a show, a stage show.
Oh, you played for the acts.
We played for the acts. And we played -- then Lester, then, would go on the stage with his father and his mother and Irma and Lee with the saxophone act.
Yeah.
And we would stay down there in the pit with the drums and the trumpet and things, to back them up.
I see. Yeah. Yeah, I see. They were part of the act, and they were part of the pit band.
Yeah.
Yeah, I see. Well, was there anybody else in the pit band?
Yeah. I can't remember them.
But some other instruments, huh?
Yeah.
A couple of other people.
I can't remember them.
No. But probably like bass and --
Yeah.
-- guitar and stuff, or maybe even banjo, huh?
Yeah. I can't remember nobody but, you know, the family.
Yeah. Well, so you didn't actually get
up on the stage with them, then?
No. But you were cutting that music, though. You were reading.
Uh-huh.
Which must have surprised them, huh?
No, but he -- see, that old man liked me. Lester's father liked me from the get-go. He liked my playing.
Yeah.
And that's the reason why he wanted me.
Yeah.
And my father talked to him. Yes, he wanted me very badly. So -- cause that's how I happened to --
Did you learn anything from him? From the father?
No.
Was he talented?
Yeah. Very talented.
Oh, he was?
Yeah.
Well, what kind of tone did he get?
He got a legitimate tone.
Oh, I see.
He wasn't nothing like Lester.
No.
Lester was something else.
Yeah. I mean, he didn't have a feel for jazz, then, the father?
No.
Oh, I see. Just the two boys, then, did. Did the girl?
Just Lester, I think. Mama could play and Lee could play.
And mama could play?
Yeah.
Really?
Yeah. All of them could play.
Well, I'll be darned. Fancy that. That's extraordinary, isn't it?
Yeah.
Well, that's very interesting. Well that was -- so that was like good breaking in, for getting experience.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well that was good. So your father really did understand how you felt. He understood what's what with you, what you wanted.
Yeah.
Didn't he?
Yeah. He definitely did.
I mean, he was in your corner.
Yeah.
Well, that's good, isn't it?
Uh-huh.
It's very good. Well, okay. Well, let's go back.

Well, he seen that the only thing that I wanted was the trumpet and music, see. And that he didn't have to make me study or do anything. Sometimes on Sundays, he would have to take the trumpet from me.
Yeah.
And lock it up in the closet.
Why? How many hours a day would you blow?
I'd just blow it all the time.
Really?
Yeah.
(Laughter)
Really. Is that right. Well, I'll be darned.
So there was these kids, see, their parents would have to get after them to practice.
Yeah. To make them practice.
Yeah.
Yeah.
But not me. They'd have to stop me.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, did you -- what about -- did you have neighbors, pals, or guys that you ran around with on the street? Or --
No.
You just really had your mind on music, didn't you?
Yeah.
Honestly?
That's right.
You didn't go out with any girls or anything?

No. I'll tell you the reason why. My father, when I got big enough to go out and play dances with bands, my father would go with me. And as soon as the dance would be over, he'd bring me back home. I never did get a chance to go out with girls.
Well --
Until I left home, to go down to Florida.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, I think -- I mean, when you think that your father was a gambling man, it's amazing how strict he was, then, about everything.
Yeah. Very strict. Very strict on me.
I guess the thing was that he knew that life very well, and he decided that you weren't going to have that life.
That's right. And another thing he was strict on, you had to be in that house before 12:00 o'clock.
Is that right?
Yeah. All of us.
Fancy that. Well, that's remarkable, isn't it?
Yeah.
Yeah.
He wouldn't care if it was the oldest one, or any one of us, we had to be in that house before 12:00 o'clock at night.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, so -- all right, then, from Eagle Eye Shields, you went down to Florida, you joined Alonzo Ross.
Yeah. I was in Florida.
Oh. Oh, yeah, of course, because you were in Jacksonville.
Uh-huh.
Well, Alonzo Ross was playing where?
Alonzo Ross was playing in Miami, at
the Della Robia.
What was that? A nightclub?
A nightclub on Second Avenue down there. A colored nightclub. And Edmund Hall joined his band. And he wanted me, too. So we left Eagle Eye and went with Alonzo Ross.
Well, who else was in that band?
Uh, who else was in that band? I remember Fulbright, the bass player.
That's Fulbright that went with Chick later on, huh?
Yeah. Yeah. Fulbright. He went with Teddy Hill.
Oh.
You remember Teddy Hill. He used to wear the big hat and clown. Yeah, he went with Teddy Hill.
So he didn't go with Chick?
No.
Oh.
Him and -- who else can I remember?
Well, how many pieces were in the band?
I think he had 12.
Oh, he did?
12 pieces.
He had the sections, then.
Yeah.
So what did you play? You were playing third trumpet, huh? Or were you playing some first?
I think we only had two trumpets.
Oh, I see.
So we used to broadcast.
Oh, for goodness' sake.

Some radio station over there on the beach, Miami Beach. And that wasn't something that you heard of, because there wasn't no colored allowed over there on the beach, then. And so they used to sneak us over there to the radio station and sneak us back.
No kidding? Really?
Uh-huh. And so that's how the fellow heard us in New York. He heard the band, the fellow that owned the Rosemont Ballroom in Brooklyn.
He heard the band over the air?
Yeah. So he came down and listened to the band. So he hired the band. You know, two weeks.
No kidding.
That's how I happened to get to New York.
All right. Let's pause a moment.
There we go. Well, Cootie, who arranged
how the band would travel up to New York? How did that happen, come up by boat?
Well, I don't know that end of the business, you know.
Yeah.
But I know that we went to Georgia. When we got to Georgia --
From --
From --
From Miami.
Yeah. And got on that boat and come to New York.
Well, what -- my geography's terrible -- what boat would you get on? I mean, how would you come from Georgia?
In Savannah, Georgia.
But what would that be, coming up the coast, or what?
Yeah.
Really?
Yeah.
No kidding. What kind of a boat? What do you remember about it?
I don't remember nothing about that boat.
Had you ever been on a boat before?
No.
You didn't get sick, huh?
I didn't care how I got to New York.
You would just know you were going to New York.
Because, Helen, when I used to say my prayers at night, I used to say, "Dear Lord, please hurry up and let me grow up so I can get to New York."
(Laughter)
I didn't care how I got there. I was coming.
(Laughter)
Well, where did you land? Do you remember?
Yeah, we landed down at the pier, some pier down here.
In Manhattan someplace.
Then we were shuffled off to Brooklyn.
Yeah.
Though I didn't know Brooklyn from any other part of New York.
No.
So we were staying over in Brooklyn, at some lady's house. So we finished the two weeks --
Well, what was it like? What was the Rosemont like? I don't remember that.
The Rosemont Ballroom? It was --
Something like the Roseland?
Yeah. Something like Roseland.
Pretty big?
Yeah.
Yeah. And they had popular bands there? Williams
Yeah. Fess Wiggins used to play there.
Really?
Yeah. Other bands used to play there.
Did they -- they didn't have a broadcast from there, did they? They didn't have a line in there did they?
No.
No.
I don't think so.
Yeah. But, so you went in for two weeks.

Yeah. So after the two weeks they were ready to go back. I said, "Not me." I said, "This is the place I've wanted to be all my life. I'm not thinking about going back to no Florida." And Helen, we was -- I was with the biggest band in the State of Florida. Colored band. And during that time, it was a cooperative band, making $150.00 a week during them times.
Good heavens.
Yeah.
When Chick was at the Savoy, they were making $35.00 a week.
That's right.
Yeah. When you split that --
In other words, you were splitting the profits.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And I didn't have nothing to go to here. But I didn't go back with them. Me and Edmond Hall stayed.
Did you have any cash in your pocket?
Yeah. I had a little cash. I used to send my father all my money.
Yeah.
My father had lost all my money, his money, everybody's money.
Oh.

So I wrote home for some money and my father sent me $50.00. And after all that was gone, I wrote home for some more money. My father told me he didn't have no more money. And I found a place in Brooklyn. Me and Edmond Hall found a place in Brooklyn where there was a baker's shop,
where we used to get our breakfast for a dime. And you used to get rolls and coffee for a dime.
Like the day before's rolls?
No. We used to eat in there.
Oh, fresh rolls?
We used to eat in there. We used to get rolls and coffee for a dime.
Yeah. That wasn't bad.
And for our lunch we used to get soup and bread for 15 cents. And that's what we ate for a long time.
No dinner?

That was our dinner. So we don't know -- so we run into some people and they say, "So what are you guys doing?" A musician, I think, one of the guys was. "They ain't doing nothing, man." "We need a job." Said, "Why don't you all go over to New York?" We said, "We're in New York."
(Laughter)

So they said, "No, go over to Manhattan. They have jam sessions over at the Bandbox, for different nights. They have trumpet night, saxophone night, piano players' night, trombone night." So we goes over there and we find out what night. So I go in there and -- trumpet night.
Where was the Bandbox?
The Bandbox was at 131st, I think, between Lenox and Seventh, near Seventh Avenue.
Yeah.

Yeah. So I go in there one night, with my trumpet, on trumpet night, and I started blowing. Somebody go get Chick Webb. Somebody went and got Chick Webb. And he listened to me play. "Where you come from, boy?"
(Laughter)
And I told him the story, after I got through blowing.
Did you know who you were talking to?

No. I didn't know who I was talking to. So he says, "Well, come on. I'll go over there to get your things." I said, "I owe the landlady money. I have to pay the landlady before I can get out." So he went over and he paid the landlady up and I moved in with him.
No kidding.
Yeah.

-- and we're going to go back and see -- I wonder why there's a line on that thing somewhere. Yes, I hear something making a noise. I wonder if that thing -- no. Okay, Cootie, you say you told Chick you owed the landlady.
Yeah. So Chick said, 'Well, that's okay. Come on#.' He took me over in a taxicab.
Took you over in a taxicab. Well, how come he had so much cash on hand?
I don't know. He wasn't working. And we went over there and picked up my bags, paid the landlady.
What about Edmond Hall? He wasn't with you?
No.
You'd gone alone.
Yeah. Because it was trumpet night.
Yeah.
And they didn't allow saxophone players in there.
Yeah.
On trumpet night.
Yeah.
I don't know if Edmond Hall was with me or not. He could have been with me.
Yeah. But anyway, you --
So we went on back over there.
Well, what were you thinking of a guy like Chick, like that? That was terrific, wasn't it?
Oh, yeah. So --
That was --
I moved in with him.
Well, when did you first hear him play some drums?
Not until we got the job at the Savoy. I think it was about a week later.
Well, that must have thrilled you when you heard him play drums, didn't it?
Yeah. Well, no instrument thrilled me but the trumpet.
Oh, Cootie, honestly? No kidding.
I don't think so. Not doing that era. Nothing thrilled me but the trumpet.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, were you a few years younger than Chick?
Yeah.
So he was really taking you under his wing?
Yeah.
What kind of a place was he living in?
He was living right across the street from the Bandbox.
Oh, he was. What'd he have, one room?
Yeah. He had one room. And his guitar player used to live there.
Trueheart.
Trueheart.
He had another room. Trueheart had another room?
Yeah. Trueheart had another room, and I was living with Trueheart.
Oh, I see. And Chick was paying both rents.
Yeah. He wasn't paying but one rent.
Oh, yeah. I see.
And Ginger. He was a musician.
Who?
What was his name? Ginger. I don't know his last name.
No, I don't either.
Was he a piano player? I don't remember.
Yeah.
So he had the house. He had the apartment.
Oh, I see. So you were renting from him.
No, I wasn't renting from nobody.
No, but they were renting from him.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So --
So did you have any cash on you at all?
No.
Nothing.
Didn't have nothing.
But Chick wanted you to blow with the band?
Yeah. So --
Did you rehearse all the time? Did you get your horn out and blow all the time in the house?
Yeah. It was a In the musicians' house. There wasn't nobody staying there but musicians.
No kidding.
And -- well, they used to have free breakfasts over there in the Bandbox.
They did? For musicians.
For musicians. They had rolls and coffee.
No kidding.
Sweet rolls and coffee.
Who ran the Bandbox then? Do you remember?
Yeah. A fellow by the name of Major. He ran the Bandbox.
And he liked musicians.
Yeah. He was a trumpet player himself.
Oh.

Eventually he studied to be a lawyer. And so I used to go and get my breakfast, free breakfast every morning. So Edmond Hall -- I think he was still over in Brooklyn -- so Edmond Hall came over on saxophone night, so they heard him.
Playing clarinet.
Playing clarinet and what else -- clarinet and alto I think he was playing. So he got a job with the piano player down at Roseland. What was his name? He was from Washington.
Claude Hopkins.
Claude Hopkins.
Yeah.
He got a job with Claude Hopkins.
Oh, he did.
So he was all straight. So while he -- before he got the job with Claude Hopkins, the little money I was making with Chick, I would help him out.
I see. Yeah. And then did he help out when he got a job, or were you working too?
I was working.
Yeah. Well, you were making $35.00 a week with Chick?
Yeah.
That was scale. At the Savoy.
That was big money during those days.
Yeah. Because Chick was only making $45.00, I think.
Yeah. That was big money. $35.00 a week was a whole lot of money in those days.
Well, let's see, now, in the band there was Trueheart.
Yeah.
Who was the bass player?
I can't remember the bass player. There was a bass player in there. Buford?
I don't know.
I think his name was Buford.
I can check that out with -- and then -- was it Big Greene on trombone?
No.
Who was it, then?
Was it Sandy?
No. Not that early. I don't think so. He did have Big Greene with him, you know. And Johnny wasn't in the band.
No.
Was -- who was the piano player? Not Fulford. That was months later, wasn't it?
No. Who was the piano player there?
A Mexican name?
No. I think Johnny Hodges' brother in law.
Who was his brother in law?
I can't think of his name.

Isn't that funny. I tell you what we'll do. When we take a pause, we'll look it up, to get that personnel. And then we'll put it on tape here, so we've got that. Because that's interesting, that first band you were with with Chick. In fact, I think it's in that article that you and I did. But we'll look it up. We won't bother now. We'll go on from there. I mean, so nobody in the band impressed you that much, but you were kind of thrilled with the band, though, weren't you? With Chick's band then?
Yeah.
Not too, huh?
Yeah.
All you wanted to do was blow.
Yeah. All I wanted to do was blow.
Yeah.
All I wanted to do was blow.
Well, listen, I want to ask you about something. When like Chick was sitting in front of you on the drums. Was he then?
