Whoever the road manager was that day.
Oh, yeah. That's right.
But we always came back to the Cotton Club, though.
Every year?
Yeah. We never did leave for good.
No.
They'd have a band in there. Maybe whoever was in there would just work until we got out of our thing and came back.
And then you came back and did a new show.
Yeah. We'd come back all the time.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, that was good, because it meant that you had a home base.
Yeah.
You haven't told me when you and Catherine married.
We got married in 1929.
Oh. Well, then, did you get married before you went with Duke?
No. I think we got married after I went with Duke.
Oh. I see. Well, that's good. So -- and did you -- did Johnny marry too, about that same time?
Johnny was already married.
Johnny was already married.
Yeah.
Yeah.
To his first wife.
Yeah. Right. When -- well, when did Chick get married? Do you remember?
No.
He wasn't married when you were with him then?
No. He didn't get married until late. Until after Ella was with him and he got rolling good.
Oh, yeah. And things looked a little--
Yeah. That's when he got married.
Yeah. Okay. Well, I think maybe you did make that first film, sometime. Maybe in '30 or '31. The Amos and Andy film, do you think?
Yeah. That's right.
Well what was that like? Going out to Hollywood and --
Oh, it was very exciting.
It was?
Yeah. It really was very exciting to
us. Going to Hollywood to make a picture, a movie with Amos and Andy. That was very big for us.
Well, I mean, actually, I don't think any jazz bands -- well, maybe Whiteman had been in a film. But I don't think any other jazz bands had been, had they?
I don't know. I don't think so.
I don't think so either.
But it was very, very exciting to us to be working with Amos and Andy.
Yeah. I'll bet.
You know, in the movies.
Yeah.
Going to Hollywood.
Sure.
(Laughter)
Yeah. It must have been terrific. And then like shooting the sequences and everything, did they -- I mean was it dubbed, or how was it done? Was it recorded live, or how was it done? Do you remember?
I don't remember, off hand.
Because they couldn't have had -- the equipment wasn't the same in those days. I think you had to -- I think they got the music down, and then you had to go through it.
Yeah.
I believe. I think that's how it was.
Yeah.
And then you had some very good picture calls, remember? There were some very good band pictures out of that period.
Yeah.
With everybody showing their teeth.
Yeah.
(Laughter)
Remember?
It was a very exciting time.
Yeah. Well, that was good. That was wonderful. Well, everything for the band was going very big then. Because it was one thing after another. The records were going very big.
Yeah.
And I guess Duke was writing a lot of hits.
Yeah.

Although, I don't think he'd written -- I don't think he had the big hits then -- by then. I don't think he had "Mood Indigo" or "Sophisticated Lady". They hadn't been written then, I don't think. Had they?
No, I don't think so. A little later on, it was, I think.
I think when the band went to England, that was prior to those numbers, I think.
Yeah.

Well, Cootie, what do you remember about that? I know that Ellington always swore he'd never cross the ocean. And then they got him fixed up where he had to go. I know he stayed high on brandy and champagne or something, all the way. Do you remember?
Yeah. We used to play cards all night long. Poker.
(Laughter)
What, rather than sleep?
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. He'd sit up, and he'd be drinking brandy and champagne. In those days I wasn't drinking.
Oh, you weren't?
No.
No kidding. Did you -- you mean from the very beginning you didn't drink? When you were a kid, right on?
No. I didn't drink until I got my band.
Not at all?
No. Not at all.
Well, isn't that extraordinary. Well,
Tricky drank, didn't he?
Yeah.
So you and Tricky hung out together, but you didn't drink?
We didn't exactly hang out together.
Oh. It was more the musical thing.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And I didn't drink then, during that time.
Did Johnny?
I don't recall Johnny drinking.
No. I guess he didn't really drink much either, did he?
No. Johnny and Barney. I don't recall anyone in there but Sonny, and who else? And Tricky.
Toby?
Yeah.
Yeah.
Toby.
And Freddy?
No.
Oh. He didn't drink either, huh?
No.
Oh. Well, Duke used to drink.
Yeah. Duke.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, that's quite unusual isn't it?
Yeah.
Or it would look unusual today, anyway.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well -- No, I didn't drink at all until I got my band.

Well, I'll be darned. Well, okay. Save that. We'll come back to that later. Just a minute now. Well, listen, then what did -- it must have seemed kind of exciting to be going to England, though. I think the band was one of the first that went to England. In fact, I can't think who went to England before it. I don't know that anybody did.
No, they had bands going to England.
Did they?
Uh-huh.
Well, I guess --
I can't remember their names.
Yeah. I guess there were bands that weren't very well known.
Yeah.
Well, anyway, it must have seemed pretty thrilling for everybody.
Yes, it was.
And then tell me about -- I know it was a surprise when you found all the fans knew you and knew the things you'd made, and what you played and everything. Do you remember that?

Oh, yeah. I never will forget that. Because when we got off the boat, and when we got to the hotel and went out, everybody knew you. The same as in America. They knew you better than the people did in America. And they would invite you to their home, and they had all your records. Knew what to talk about. Knew when you were born, what was the first record you ever made.
(Laughter)
Isn't that amazing.
Yeah.
Because they didn't in America.
No.
In those days. The fans really didn't know, did they.
Well, they still don't know.
No.
Not here in America.
Yeah.
On jazz.
Yeah.

See, on jazz, the people in Europe, they're very well educated on jazz, which the American public are not. Any place you go in Europe, the general public are very much educated. On jazz music. That's something that we don't have here in America.
Yeah.

I think the influence is the disc jockeys here in America, the reason why the people don't know about jazz music. I think about five -- about seven years ago, they introduced a course in the major universities and colleges on jazz. Just about seven years ago.
Yeah.
That's the reason why.
And that's about 30 years later than what we're talking about.
Yeah.

Yes, I guess that's it, isn't it. Well, maybe it's that the whole thing is that it's always pretty well been here that what's making the dollar is what people are going to talk about. And, I mean, jazz wasn't something that was considered a real money maker. Not compared to -- well, compared to the Wayne Kings and the Guy Lombardos, and people like that. Right?
Right. [Right on.]
And the disc jockeys, they usually line
right up with whatever is selling.
That's right.
You know. And so -- I mean, it's the same way today, isn't it? Whatever the kids are buying, that's what the disc jockeys --
Are playing.
-- are going to be telling them about.
That's right.

That's it, yeah. Well, listen, if I remember correctly, that first trip to England was the first time the band had ever gave a concert. I think -- you were playing a theater or something. I may be wrong on this, Cootie, but I remember that you had to give a Sunday afternoon concert, in a concert hall. And that's when Constant Lambert was there, the big classical composer, and so on. And did -- you know, he wrote a lot of wonderful things about the band and about Duke as a composer. And I think that was the first time that the band got up on stage and performed as a concert. Do you remember that?
I can't remember it, you know. Too clearly.
No.
But we had been playing theaters, and theaters are similar to concert.
Yeah. That's right. But not -- but in

those days, to play a theater, you're playing a show. And you've got it routined as a show, you know. You have an opener, and you feature this and that and the other thing, and you end up with a -- you know, you close the show with something and so on.
Not in that other period.
No? Tell me about it.
When we played the Palace Theater, we was an act.
Oh, you were part of the show that was at the theater.
That's right.
What would you have, about 35 minutes, do you think?
Yeah. And we played our music.
Yeah.
All around New York we had played theaters. And we played an act, with our music.
But you would close the bill?
Yeah.
You did close it.
We were the stars.
Yeah.
On the show.
Yeah.
We played all the theaters that was open in New York, and around.
Yeah. And then you always had to come back and play a couple of encores.
Yeah.
Because you were closing the bill.
That's right.

Yeah. Well, that's really what I mean, in a way, Cootie. Because -- so, as you say, it was an act, and it was the last act on the bill. And if I remember rightly, you know, there was quite a lot of things written by the critics and by some of the serious critics in the London press, and an arrangement was made to play an actual concert on a concert stage, in a concert hall.
I recall that now.
You remember it?
Yeah. I remember it now.
It was the first time you ever did it.
Yeah.
The band ever did that. And it was very, very thrilling. And the people knew exactly what they were listening to, and what they were hearing, and it was -- you had an absolute ovation. Remember?
Uh-huh.
I think Jack Hylton arranged it or something.
You know, made it possible. Because it was a last minute thing.

Well, I'll tell you one thing. It's a pleasure to play for people that understand your music and understand what you're doing. Now, sometimes you play here in America, and the people don't understand your music and what you're doing. Because they don't know jazz. They don't know nothing about jazz, some people that come to concerts. And some of the universities and things we played, some of them have never heard of Duke Ellington. You know.
You mean the younger generation today.
The younger generation. Yeah.
Yeah.
They don't know nothing about jazz.
Yeah.
And it's kind of hard to play to an audience, you know, that don't know nothing about jazz.
Yeah.
And so it's a pleasure to play in Europe.
Yeah.
All over Europe.
Yeah.
And people know all about jazz.
Yeah. Well, you didn't -- I don't think you went to France that first trip, did you?
I don't think so.

I don't believe so. But I know what you did do, if you can remember. Well, I was thinking about the Prince of Wales, but there was also the Prince George, who became King of England. He, too, was at a party. As you say -- you said some millionaire, or some magnate, some tobacco magnate or something.
Yeah.
Gave a big private party in his tremendous home.
Yeah.
Or estate, or whatever it was. And the Prince of Wales was present, right?
That's right.
And then, his younger brother, who became King George --
I don't remember him too much, but --
Well, I think one of them -- didn't one of them play some drums?
Yeah. The Prince of Wales.
Was it the Prince of Wales?
Yeah. He got on Sonny's drums and beat the drums at the party that night.
Did he?
He was always around. We used to see him quite often.
Did you?
Yeah.

Isn't that funny? Well, you know, I don't know if you remember that story, but there was a story about they were entertaining Duke or welcoming him or something, or he was at the bar or something, and the Prince of Wales asked Duke, 'What are you drinking? What are you going to have?' You know. And I think the thing was champagne, or a scotch and soda or something, and Duke said -- I think he said he'd have a pink gin or something.
(Laughter)
And the Prince of Wales said, you know, 'I'll have a pink gin, too.' I know Duke had some funny stories about things that went on. But they really had a very warm reception for the band, didn't they?
Oh, yeah. Palladium Theater, that's what it was.
Yeah.
We opened at the Palladium.

That's right. Well, Cootie, let's see. That takes us to, I think about -- well, that was in '33. So in '34, let's start to think when Duke started to put some more people in the band. Now, I don't know how well we're going to
do about dates here, but when he started to augment the band, because -- for instance, when you went with the band, was Artie in it then?
Yeah.
And Posey?
Yeah.
Oh. And sort of being the three -- you mean, they toured with Bubber?
Yeah.
I see.
I had taken Bubber Miley's place.
Yeah. So there were three trumpets and the one trombone.
Yeah.
Well, it seems to me that one of the first people he put on was Lawrence.
Lawrence? No, I think it was Tizol, wasn't it? I can't recall which one came first.
Well --
It was Lawrence or Teazie.
I remember Lawrence made that 'Shiek of Araby,' remember?
Yeah.
That caused a lot of talk.
Uh-huh.
Well, let's see. The four saxophones. It was quite a while before Ben came in the band.
Yeah.

That was quite a long while, I think, because I think that was around 1940 that Ben first came in the band, I believe. But, let's see, who else? When did Freddy drop out of the band? Can you remember?
I don't recall when Freddy dropped out of the band. I don't remember.
Well, I know he was there when you went to England.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, he was there.
Yeah.
I think his wife was taken real sick, and that's the reason why he quit.
Right. Oh, I know what we haven't talked about. When Ivy came with the band. Ivy was with the band when you played the Palladium, wasn't she? Or was she that first time? No, Well, maybe she wasn't.
I don't think so.
We didn't have a singer, did we?
No.
Well, then, I -- I can look that up, too,
because I'll look up Ivy here. But it seems to me that that was about the next thing. Ivy was playing at the Grand Terrace.
Yeah.
And Earl was doing the show, and Ivy was a soubrette or something.
Yeah. She was --
And you were playing the theater?
Yeah.
The band was doing -- and you had a terrific show.
Oriental.
At the Oriental.
Uh-huh.
And I guess Duke had never had a girl -- well, he had never had a singer at all, had he?
I don't think so.
I don't either.
I really can't recall.
Yeah. Well --
When did Herb Jeffries come with him?
Afterwards, I think.
Yeah?
Yes. I feel so. I believe so.
Yeah.

Well, let's talk about -- I did a piece on Ivy, and I remember her telling about when she -- when she went out with the band, when she came out on the stage at the Oriental, how scared she was. And she was so scared she wasn't going over very well. And then Sonny started shouting from the drums, and the people all laughed and she relaxed and everything happened, you know, and it all came off beautifully. And that really established it, didn't it?
Yeah.
Because -- I mean, Ivy was always -- in a sense, wouldn't you say it was like an act? Ivy coming on with the band was, in a sense, like an act. I mean, she came on -- there was humor.
Yeah.
First, she was gowned.
Yeah.
She was well gowned.
Yeah.
And there was good humor and humor -- I mean, she didn't come on singing a ballad.
No. She was a great entertainer.
Or it wasn't romance and this and that. But it was a gay thing where she and Duke worked off one another.
Uh-huh.
And so on. And then Sonny always got in that act.
Yeah. It was well planned, really. Well rehearsed.
Yeah.
Between Irving Mills and different producers and different things, they staged the thing properly.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So really what it meant was that the act, the band, in theaters, changed to the extent that it closed with the girl singer, didn't it?
I don't remember how it closed.
Don't you?
No.
No Well, maybe it didn't.
I don't think so.
Maybe she just came on at the end.
Yeah.
And did her three numbers, or maybe four -- came back and did a fourth.
Yeah.
And then the band --
The band closed it.
-- came on with their thing. Yeah. That's
right. Well, what did it seem like, with a gal starting to travel with the band? That was --
She fit right in.
Did she?
(Laughter)
Yeah.
She even played cards, do you recall?
Yeah. She fit right in. Played poker with us on the train.
Really?
We'd set up and she'd be right there playing poker. Yeah.
Isn't that funny? Well, then, Ivy was with the band for a long time.
Yeah.
What, about ten years, I think, wasn't it?
I think so.
Yeah. I think so too. Did Ivy quit because she got sick, or did she quit because she really wanted to settle down on the West Coast? Do you remember?
I wasn't there when she left.
Oh, you weren't.
No.
Oh.
I don't recall that.

Yeah. Well, okay. Let's see what else changed -- what else had some significance in the band happened during that time. Really, the best way for us to figure that out, Cootie, is for me to get a listing of those records. If we look through, as those records were released, that's what will bring it back to our minds, what happened. Because, for instance, you look at "Cottontail", you know that Ben was in the band, etcetera.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
There was "Perdido" and "Cottontail", but I think those -- well, the war --
Okay, Cootie. Let's say something. Let's get a shot on you.
Yeah. Okay.
All right, now. We'll try and --

I'm talking to Cootie Williams again. May 13th. This is Helen Dance, and we're going to pick up where we left off. Cootie, we were just at the point where you joined Duke. That was '29, and I guess it was at the Cotton Club. And what I'd like you to tell me is, in those days, how it was in the band. It was different from what it got to be afterwards.

Yeah. It was quite different. Everyone in the band would pitch in and help write songs, everything that, almost, Duke did in those days. Someone in the band helped to do them. And in later years, I mean it got a little different, and people stopped doing things like that because they wasn't paid for them properly.
Yeah.
We only got $25.00 for a song if we gave it to him.
No kidding.
Uh-huh.
You mean it was a song, and maybe it was going to be recorded and everything, and that was it, huh? That's all it meant.
Yeah. That's all it meant. And one of the biggest things that I did there was 'Concerto for Cootie'. I had to beg him to take that.
I didn't even know that. Really?
(Laughter)
No kidding. Really?
Yeah. That happened to be a way up in the million dollar seller.
So you mean, even so your name didn't get on the number.
No.
If your name had got on the number, you would have shared in those royalties, wouldn't you?
No. He had bought the song.
Oh, I see.
All of us used to sell the songs to him for $25.00.
Yeah.
And some of the fellows, in later years, they sued him.
Did they? Who did?
(Laughter)
Who did? Can you remember anybody?
Yeah. Barney Bigard for 'Mood Indigo'.
No kidding. Did he get anywhere with it?
Yeah. He got money.
He did?
"Boy Meets Horn."
Rex Stewart and (unintelligible). But I didn't do it.
Well --
No. I believed in if I sold a person something and he paid for it, I didn't believe in going back, you know, and saying that I didn't mean it that way.
Yeah.
So I let it go. It was fun then. You

Well, I guess in the beginning there, when nobody knew what the future was going to be, and it was so exciting and everything, it was -- well, in a sense, the band was almost like a cooperative band in the beginning, wasn't it in a way?
Yeah. In a way it was, you know. And it was a pleasure, you know, to have the band to play your song.
Yeah.
To hear someone playing your song. And that's the reason we did it.

Yeah. Well, then, Cootie, another way that things got written, if I remember correctly, was on the record sessions, because a lot of times, I mean, Duke would start off with the blues or something, and then somebody would say, 'Hey, here's eight bars,' or something.
Yeah.
And somebody would say, 'Let's do this for a middle.' Right?
Yeah.
For the release and so on, I mean, things got put together by virtue of two or three people.
That's right. But 'Concerto for Cootie' was me alone.
Yeah.
And with him. He did the verse on it or something.
He did?
Yeah. But the part at the release, "Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me", was all me. Was all of my writing.
Had he ever heard you play it or anything?
No.
Had you ever played it over for him?
No.
So you wrote out the song and gave it to him, huh?
Yeah. I stood on the bus -- got right down there on the steps of the bus from Boston to New York, begging him to buy this song for $25.00.
(Laughter)
Well, what did he say? He didn't know if he was going to like it?
Yeah. A whole lot of jive. I don't know.
(Laughter)
Really?
And about the time we got to New York, he said, "Well, okay. I'll buy it."
Isn't that funny? Well, Cootie, I mean don't you think a lot of times he enjoyed himself that way, anyway?
Well, yes. He did.
He probably knew he was going to buy it anyway.
Yeah. Probably so. But I think in those days, there was a lot of things being created in the band. Because everyone would pitch in and do things.
Yeah.
But they found out the value of it. Then they stopped doing these things for nothing.
Yeah. Well, I mean, that makes sense, doesn't it?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Well, like "Sophisticated Lady". There were about three people writing on that, weren't there?
Yeah.
Didn't Toby have one of those -- Otto
Yeah. I think he also had something in that.
Yeah. And there was somebody else.
I don't know if Lawrence Brown was on it or not. I don't know.
No. I don't remember. But I don't think
Toby got anywhere with it, though, as far as I remember.
No.
That's funny, isn't it? And then there must have been an awful lot of things of Johnny's.
Oh, yeah. An awful lot of things of Johnny's.
Yeah. Well, "Song out of My Heart," wasn't that a counter melody on something else?
I can't remember.
I don't remember. Well, it seems to me it had something to do with "In a Mellow Tone."
"X Don't Get Around Much Anymore".
Really?
I don't know.
Was it tied in with that?
Yeah, I think so.
Yeah. Well, of course, another thing was in those days, Duke didn't do those lyrics himself. Not in the early days, did he?
No.
So I mean, a lot of times, unless he got a lyric writer, well nobody knew whether the number was going to mean anything or not. It was an instrumental.
That's right.
Isn't that right?
Yeah. It was an instrumental. The first record that came out on "Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me", was "Concerto for Cootie".
Yeah. That's right. And I think a long time passed before he got the lyrics to "Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me". I think it was about a year and a half later.
Yeah.
Doesn't it seem to you it was a long time?
Yeah. But when they reissued "Concerto for Cootie" --
Yeah.
To "Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me".
Oh, was it?
The same song, yeah.
Oh. And he had a singer on it.
No. It was me, playing the same solos. Playing the same things.
Oh. But just the title.
Yeah. Just the title.
Well then, afterwards, when that began to take, well it seems to me it was when Joya was in the band or something. Which of the girls -- one of the girls sang that all the time.
I don't know. I think it was Hibler, wasn't it?
Oh, yes, maybe it was. Because it was earlier than when those three girls were with the band, wasn't it?
Uh-huh.
Yeah. It probably was Hibler. Yeah. Well I -- I mean, that was your big -- that was your first big number that was all written around you, the whole number, wasn't it?
I think so. I think so, yeah.

It seems to me, Cootie, that that was one of the first numbers that was written around one musician in the band. Then after that, he had a number for Barney. I don't remember which it was, but -- "Clarinet Lament".
"Clarinet Lament". Yeah.
And then he had -- well, he had a real beautiful ballad or something for Johnny, didn't he? "Warm Valley", or something like that. I think there was -- let me just --
I think Billy Strayhorn used to do all of Johnny's things, didn't he?
Did he?
I think so. I don't know.
You mean he used to score them.
Yeah.
Do the arrangement. Yeah, I think he --
He used to write all the things for Johnny.
You mean, in other words, Johnny had all of those -- those melodies were things that Johnny played here and there, weren't they? Things that --
I don't know. I wasn't there. But it's my understanding that -- well, I know when I was there, Billy Strayhorn only wrote for Johnny Hodges.
Yeah. Yeah, that's right. That's right. Well, let me see. Just let me check this and make sure this is going all right.
Yeah.

Well, Cootie, I think it might not be a bad idea if we started talking about some of those records that were made, from the time that you first went with the band. For instance, in January 1930, I guess that was the first session you made with the band. I'll tell you what titles were on that. "Rent Party Blues" was on it, and "Jungle Blues". And "St. James Infirmary". There was a fourth number, but I don't think I have that down. But that was the first session that you made with them. "Jungle Blues" I guess you were perhaps using the plunger. Do you recall that at all?
No. I don't recall that.
I mean, that's only oh, going to be a
blues.
Yeah.

I don't think it was ever remade or anything. But anyway, it was first. But in April in 1930, that was a very good session. And incidentally, Tizol Teazle came in the band in '29. Last time, when you and I talked about it, I thought Teazle came quite a bit later than that, but he must have come in about the same time you did.
He came in after me, though.
He came in after you.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, on that session -- it was a very good session. It was "Ring Dem Bells". Remember?
Yeah. I remember "Ring Dem Bells".
And Sonny calling out in that. That was a good number, wasn't it?
Yeah.
And "Three Little Words" also was a good one.
Yeah.
And then you made "The Mooch", and that featured you.
That featured me. I was using the plunger then.
Yeah. So that was in April. So you joined
the band in November, '29, didn't you?
Yeah. Something like that.
So four months later you were already that familiar with the plunger.
Yeah.

Well, listen. Just while we're talking about that, the plunger, one time when you and I were doing an interview earlier, you started talking to me about the plunger. Well, first of all, last time we talked you laughed about it and said that it seemed like funny to you. But afterwards, you told me that that just became a part of you.

Yeah, it did become a part of me, because that was what Duke Ellington hired me to do. And it dawned on me. I had taken Bubber Miley's place, and that was Bubber Miley's trademark, the plunger. And I was almost a legit trumpet player at that time. I had just left Fletcher Henderson's band, playing first trumpet. And coming in -- and I never used a plunger. Then by, you know, sitting and listening to Joe Tricky Sam Nanton, that's how I picked it up.
Well, but the thing is this, you know. You were pointing out that you had like two ways of being yourself. You -- I mean, as you said, Louis was your idol. And so you used to blow open horn.
Yeah.
And you used to blow like Louis was your
inspiration. That was really the style, wasn't it. I mean, it was your interpretation of this -- that field.
That's right, isn't it, in a sense. So that was you and the you that used the plunger was another you altogether, because those two styles are -- well, they're totally different, aren't they?

Well, they're entirely different. And my advice to any youngster that's coming up, not to listen to no one individual playing. Because he will never find out his identification by listening to one individual. Listen to all jazz men, all good jazz men play. Then you will become yourself. You will play some of the things that all of them play. But you will be playing yourself.
Yeah. Yeah. And you wouldn't -- you're not necessarily meaning just listen to everybody on your own instrument, but listen to what everybody's got to say on their instrument.
Yeah. All great jazz musicians.

Yeah. Dizzy said to me one time that, you know, you listen -- you keep listening to everybody, and you keep playing what you like, what you heard that you like, and you keep playing it. And suddenly you find that, coming out of this foundation, is something that you didn't ever hear before, which is you.
Yeah.
And that's the way it is, isn't it?
That's the way it is.
It's like you get an alphabet, and then you begin to make your own sentences.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, Cootie, you listened to everybody, didn't you? Because you had that passion for trumpet players.
Yeah. I listened to all trumpet players.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Well, for instance, you know, when you say that you were really a legit man in a way, or what you played first, it's true you were playing first trumpet, but did you never get 16 bars or 32 bars or something where you were to get off on your own, up until that point?
No. Not up until that point. After I left Fletcher, when I went with Duke, then I got a chance to play solos.
Well, the few times that you worked with Chick you did play solos. Didn't you?
Yeah. Couple of times, I played solos. Yeah, with Chick I did.
I mean, Chick knew.
Yeah.
He knew.
Yeah.
He wanted to hear it.
Yeah.
He knew what was there, didn't he?
Yeah.
Yeah.
I could play solos, but when I went with Fletcher, all I had to do was to play first trumpet.
Yes.
That was a job in itself.
Yes.
To set back and play his trumpet.
Yes. That's right. And it took that much lip, too, didn't it?
Oh, yeah.

Yeah. Well, when you'd be, you know, rehearsing at home, woodshedding, or whatever, you know, blowing at home -- I guess you didn't get that much time to -- but you would -- you would improvise then, when you were on your own, wouldn't you?
Oh, yeah.
You would blow things.
Oh, yeah. Even when I had my teacher. Then I would be at home, I would study jazz and play jazz.
Yeah.
And listen to records and try to do things off of records.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, Cootie, because -- it's a funny thing, but the two styles that you've got, both styles, nobody ever really did either of them before. And I don't know whether anybody ever did them afterwards. But, first of all, we don't have to elaborate on the point that nobody played the plunger style like you. You didn't play it like Bubber anyway. And what you worked out for yourself -- Tricky Sam was an inspiration, but what you worked out was your thing. And that was that. But the way -- take, like "Concerto for Cootie". You do play open on there, don't you?
Yes, I do.

That's what I thought. Well, nobody ever -- first of all, I guess -- I don't think anybody ever had such a powerful tone. I don't think anybody ever got up and blew so strong, which was also playing jazz, not just playing a straight lead.
No.
Right?
That's right. Uh-huh.
I mean, in other words, it was like --
like playing jazz solo, which came out as strong and pure and beautiful as a first part in a way, but it was also playing jazz. That's a fact, isn't it?
Yeah. Uh-huh.

And so that that becomes -- because this was what was so impressive on that "Concerto for Cootie", so that you really drove and moved the whole band. That one voice. Everything fell in back of it. That's true, isn't it?

Well, yeah. I try to, you know, tell a story when I'm playing. This part too is very important when you're playing an instrument. And to try to tell the story of what you're playing. It's not just to play the notes.
Well, tell that -- spell that out a bit more.
Just like if you're reading a book and you're telling a story to kids, or something. And when you're playing an instrument, which I try to tell a story, when I'm blowing. In the same way.
You start, making an opening statement.
Yeah.
And from there you push your story forward.
That's right.
And then, from what came there, the next thing follows and leads on.
Uh-huh.
And then, when you get your release, the thing is like a contrast, or a new thought or a sort of thing.
Yeah.
And then, Cootie, so when you're going to play a second chorus, then you have your story, and you start to put more force to it, and more feeling to it really. It builds, doesn't it?
Yeah.

Yeah. Well that, you know, that probably accounts for the fact that more or less everything certainly that you recorded can all be sung. And, in fact, when you hear those numbers, you hear in your ear the things that you blew there.
Yeah.
It's like a song, really.
Uh-huh.
It's jazz, but it is like a song. Am I correct in thinking that?

Well, I'll tell you. Sometimes -- this is another thing -- I don't think I ever said this before. Some people play on chord construction. I don't play on chord construction. I like to have a melody. I like to read the music down, and see what the composer intended for it to be. In order for me to play it, to get a feeling out of it. Now,
You don't know what the song is.
-- the song is. What his idea is of anything.
Yeah.
Once you have a melody there, and I can see this melody and play this melody over, and see his idea, then I can improvise on this melody, to do something with it.
Yeah. Yeah. So you can make a melody on his melody, which belongs to his melody.
Right.
Right. Yeah.
But I cannot do it on chord construction.

No. No. Because after all, I mean, that is the point. You made your own melody, when you made "Concerto for Cootie". You know, there were your chord constructions and that was your own melody. And I mean, when you are playing somebody else's song, unless you see what that song itself is, it could be any series of small melodies built on those same chord progressions, couldn't it?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Yeah. I see.
That's the idea.

Yeah. Well, Cootie, and I guess in any case, the chords are that much built into you anyway, that -- I mean, all you need to do is hear the melody, read the melody and hear the melody. After that, you don't go around thinking about chords, because you know instinctively what chords --
Yeah.
-- are -- what the progression is.
Yeah.

Yeah. Well, another thing -- I mean, that's -- in those days it wasn't -- it hadn't become the fashion to fit in such an enormous number of runs and notes and to cover so much ground at such fast tempos. Or, not necessarily such fast tempos, but filling it in, you know, playing 16ths, or 32s, you know, whatever. And it was much more the thing, wasn't it, to beautify the thing by creating --
Yeah.
-- further melody to things.
Uh-huh.
I mean, that was also Duke's concept, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Because he was doing the same kind of thing on piano. He was also -- when he'd come in, he'd work in melody, he'd work melody into things, wouldn't he? He'd contribute melody to the number as well.
Well, he would -- all the time, he would give certain things to different people for what he would want.
Yeah.
He was very shrewd in that. You know. He wrote a song or something, he would give it to the person which idea that he had.
Yeah.
And what he wanted. And it always was successful, because he wrote for these different type of people.

Well, Cootie, when that was happening like that, when it was being built in the record session, which it was so often, you know. I mean, I remember those things getting themselves created as they were happening, you know. In that case, very often he didn't have a -- well, maybe he had an eight bar theme, but not more.
Yeah.

He had a theme, or maybe it was somebody's theme. Maybe it wasn't even his. But there was a theme there. But then, as he would point to you or call on you or call on Johnny or somebody, he was looking for something else to come out of it.
Yes.
For it to be built on from there.
Right.
In another color, in another sound or another feel, or maybe a progression right from what it originally was. But this is how it got itself built, isn't it?
Right.
Well, the person that -- I mean if he'd turn around and call on you, in that instance, you are working from chords.
But I have heard some type of melody.
Yeah. You know how it started out.
Yeah.
So you know what vein you're in.
Yeah.
Yeah. Right. Mostly those things were 32 bars, weren't they?
Yeah.
Because they were three minute records. So --

But I think in chord construction, the idea came in later years. The chord construction thing, for people to play on the chord. That came in later years. But in our generation, I think it was the melody. And you played off the melody, with the chord construction. But you had a foundation there of melody. Something to go by.
Yeah.
Other than the chords.
Yeah. Let's hold it a minute now.
Cootie, on that same session, you made "East St. Louis". So you were featured on that, too.
Oh, yeah. "East St. Louis" Tadd's-00. (Unintelligible)
Well, that was the theme song.
Because that was the theme.
Yeah.
Wasn't it.
That was the theme song.
Well, so, on that theme, did that get played like a chorus and then on the second chorus you were featured? Can you remember?
No.
Or were you playing plunger right from the start, in that first chorus?
Right in the first chorus.
Oh, you were. Yeah.
All the way to the end.
All the way to the end.
Yeah. All the way to the end.
Yeah. When -- was that -- where did that number come from? I've forgotten. Did Duke write all of that?
I wasn't there.
Maybe he wrote it with Bubber.
Yeah. Maybe Bubber.
I should think so, wouldn't you?
Yeah.
That was probably the real early days in the Kentucky Club or something, where they were -- where Bubber supplied something, and they made it their theme. When it was real -- just the few guys.
Yeah.
The five or six guys or whatever.
Yeah.
It's a beautiful thing. Don't you think it is?
Yeah. I liked it very much.
I always was sorry that he ever did change that theme. But still, you know -- well, not only did he use "A Train" for a theme, but he used --
That was the only two I remembered.
Was it?
That I recall, yeah.
There wasn't one between "A Train", then.
No.
Oh. So he never switched until Strayhorn was in the band then.
That's right.

And wrote. Yeah. Okay, good. Well, listen, now, in November that year, the band made "Rockin' in Rhythm", which was one of the real beautiful numbers, I think. Don't you? Don't you like that number? Or do you think it's too simple?
It was a simple number. Just a simple thing.
It's a simple [blues ], isn't it?
Yeah.
But it has a beautiful swing to it. Don't you think it does? What are you smiling for? What's your feeling about that number? Does it bore you?
No. Well, you know my solo was taken off of that and made another song.
Oh, no. I don't. Which is that?
I think Harry James taken it. And made a song called "Pecking".
No. Really?
Yeah.
I didn't know that. No, I didn't. How about that. So that's what I'm talking about when I say you do a solo that's like a song. How about that. Is that right? And no acknowledgement, no nothing.
No. And I didn't get a dime for it. I don't know if Irving Mills got paid for it.
How about that.
And I --
No lyrics went on that did they?
No.
But it was just one of Harry's trumpet numbers.
Yeah. I don't know if Duke was in on it or not.
(Laughter)
You mean you wonder, huh? Well, how about that. Because it was acknowledged then that it was. Harry acknowledged that that was what he had done, huh? Or that that's what it was, huh?
Everyone knew it.
Everybody knew it.
Because that was my solo, my plain solo, 'Rockin' in Rhythm', he'd taken that and made a song out of it.
(Laughter)
No changes?
No, no changes.
(Laughter)
Oh, isn't that something. Well, listen, my memory of 'Rockin' in Rhythm' particularly is that that was the background for Bessie Dudley's dance act with the band in
theaters. Remember?
Yeah. I think the thing came about, it was Pigmeat Markham.
Yeah.
He was playing in Philadelphia, and during rehearsals, we had to get some music for him. And they started to jiving around, and that's how "Rockin' in Rhythm" came about.
Is it really? So it was born to back up a dancer, then.
Yeah, I think it was.
Yeah. That's what it was.
Yeah. I think it was Harry Carney started playing or something. Somebody. And that's how it came about.
Yeah, because the saxophones are very -- that first chorus is saxophones, isn't it?
I don't recall.
Yeah. I think. Yeah, well, I know that Duke turned -- every time that he wanted to get something going and get it swinging, you know, on stage, he put that in, didn't he?
Yeah. During rehearsal. That's how I remember it came about. Then it just worked itself in.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, that is good. That
was a beautiful number. Well, look, then -- you know, in '30, '31, it seemed like everything that he did, you were playing a lot of plunger, because in June, '31 --
Yeah. Well, Cootie, let's just talk about "Creole Rhapsody" for a minute or two, and we'll check this one out.
"Creole Rhapsody"?
Yeah.
Oh, that's one I can't remember too well.
No kidding. That was a very big number for you. That was a good number. That was another jungle type number.
Yeah.
And I think he used clarinets on it. If I remember correctly.
I can't recall it.
Well, it was a pretty number. Well, if you don't remember that too much, we won't talk about that too much. Let's see what's happened here. Just a second.
Let's talk about in 1932, one of the big sessions was "Don't Mean a Thing". Now what's your memory on that? Who was involved in there? Can you remember? "If it
ain't got that swing." I mean, where did that come -- who did that come out of, or how did that come about? Do you think.
It came out of me.
No. Really? Did it?
Yeah. The saying. The saying I used to tell him. I used to tell Duke, I said, "Man, it don't mean a thing if it ain't got that swing."
(Laughter)
Because if it ain't got the swing, it ain't got no beat. It's got to swing.
Yeah.
Yeah. So that's how the title came about.
Yeah.
It don't mean a thing if it ain't got that swing.
Well, listen. That had to be born with words and music. That didn't get born in just music. I mean that had to come because of doo-wah, doo-wah, and all that. It came right out of it, didn't it?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
So maybe you're -- your saying that to Duke, he just simply --
He got something out of it.
He got something out of it. He -- it
just came right out on the piano. I guess that's just what happened, isn't it?

And he probably said to you, 'Doo-wah,' and you did this. You picked it up from there. After all, that's surely one of the biggest numbers he ever had. I mean, to this day, when his name's mentioned, that comes up. And it's used by other people for all kinds -- I mean, it's used by writers and it's just a truism. It's a tradition, by now. 'It Don't Mean a Thing if it Ain't Got that Swing.' So you contributed something to the English language, Cootie, with that one.
(Laughter)
Because that just applied to everything. Yeah. I guess the guys were -- I guess everybody was kind of thrilled with that, weren't they, when you made that number?
I don't think so.
No?
No.
I wonder -- you see, Ivy must have been in the band then. That wasn't made without a vocal, was it?
I don't think so.
I don't think so. I think Ivy must have been in the band. Would you -- does that seem right to you in 1932?
I don't remember the year.
I'll tell you why. Because later on in '32, in May of '32, there's "Stormy Weather", and Ivy certainly made that. Remember?
Yeah.
So she must have come in the band. While we're on that subject, you must have some -- you must remember Ivy coming in the band.
No, I don't remember what year she came in the band.
No. But you remember the Ori -- that she opened up at the Oriental theater.
Yeah. At the Oriental Theater. Yeah.
And she was scared, wasn't she?
I don't remember that.
You don't. Well, she told me that she --
Because I didn't know her then.
No.
We didn't have time to be thinking about nobody else.
(Laughter)
Everybody was all wrapped up with what they were doing.
Yeah.
On their horns.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. Well, I mean it was something, because you know, you'd never had a girl singer in the band before.
No.

And of course -- of course, Duke had a big thing about singers, didn't he? I mean, he really did love -- he loved singers, didn't he? I mean, all through his entire career he was always turning up singers.
Yeah. He --
Don't you think he did?
Yeah. He came up with, you know, singers. He liked singers, yeah.

I mean, I don't say -- I'm not saying that they're singers that you would maybe be turning up yourself. Or I mean, now Earl Hines has a thing about singers. He's turned up a number of singers. He turned up Billy Eckstine, and he turned up Sarah Vaughan, he turned up Madeleine Greene, you know, and a number of people. But with him, his thing was more, you know, legit, or more qualified singers, if I can say that. Duke had a thing about singers with a style, didn't he? That offered something. Well, because, like Hibler had his own style. Who was that boy in the -- a nice singer -- that boy at the time of "Jump for Joy". What's his name? The first boy singer, remember? A good looking boy.
Herb Jeffries?
Yeah. Herb Jeffries.
Yeah. He was very good.
He was good.
I liked him.
I did, too, yeah. He was a good singer. But not -- but nothing flashy.
No.

Or sensational. But he was a good singer. But I mean if Ivy hadn't -- if they hadn't, Duke or Sunny, if they hadn't worked up an act for Ivy, she'd have never gone over so big. To my way of thinking. What do you think?
Well, she had a lot of personality.
Yeah.
Herself. And while -- I don't think that Ivy was -- what would you say, now? A good singer on records, or vocalist. I think she was much better in person.
Yeah. Right. Right. She came across in person.
Yeah. She came across. She could put over a song.
Yeah.
Right. That's what I liked about Ivy.
Well, I mean, because actually, while Ivy
did justice to her numbers, she didn't have the beautiful voice that some singers have, you know.
No.
She didn't have the same equipment to bring that some singers did.
That's right.

And of course -- I mean, her background, before she came into the band, she was a soubrette, you know, which is sort of -- she stayed in character that way, really, didn't she? I mean, like you know, when Duke would bring her on -- well, maybe she'd do her "Stormy Weather" and things, but she would always end up with something like -- well, even later on, when Rex would do the funny -- there was always something a little gay, a little funny, a little -- to involve the audience.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah. Incidentally, though, there were -- I don't know what you would say, but I had one or two numbers of hers that I liked very much. One was "I'm Satisfied". Maybe you don't remember it, because you wouldn't play the records the same way we would, you know.
No.
But I've got it written here, somewhere. She did "And No Greater Love". And "Isn't Love the Strangest Thing". She had three or four numbers that were very, very nice, that
she just sang. They were straight numbers. They probably weren't so big on stage. He may not have even used them on stage. But they were good records. You don't remember that "I'm Satisfied"?
No, I don't remember it.
No. Well, anyway, well going on from "Don't Mean a Thing", in that same session, which was a terrific session, there was "Black and Tan".
Yeah. "Black and Tan Fantasy".
Yeah.
Yeah.
So really, Cootie, in those early days, you must have been the -- you must have had about four or five jungle numbers yourself, you know. You had "East St. Louis" and you had --
"The Mooch".
"The Mooch". And "Black and Tan".
"Black and Tan".
And there was another. Well, I'm sure -- I think you had a part on that "Creole Rhapsody". It seems to me there was another.
"Creole Love Call".
Yeah. "Creole Love Call". That's right. That's true. Well, did -- Bubba had done "Black and Tan" before you. Am I right?
Yeah.
Well, when you made that film in Hollywood, they called it "Black and -- didn't they call it "Black and Tan Fantasy", or something? The film?
Yeah.
And you -- so you made that.
Uh-huh.
You played that. Can you remember one -- what other numbers you played in that film?
No. I never would remember.
No.
We did that right here.
I thought you went to Hollywood to do that.
No.
Oh, it was the Amos and Andy thing you went to Hollywood for.
Amos and Andy picture. That's right.
Oh. You did that right here. Is that right? What, some independent producer or something.
Maybe so.
Yeah. Well, that surely gave the band a kick. It must have been the first time they were on film, huh?
Yeah.
Shot a movie.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. It was pretty short, though, wasn't it?
Yeah.

I don't think it lasted very long. I think it was only ten or twelve minutes. I don't think it was -- oh, maybe it was longer than that, but it wasn't very long, I don't think. Well, on that same session, Cootie, you did "Creole Love Call". So I'm a little -- you know, maybe the guys thought you were blowing too much.
(Laughter)
On those sessions. You know, you had quite a lot of parts to play on those. But "Creole Love Call", who comes down front on that? Two or three people come down front. Don't they?
Yeah. Three clarinets.
Yeah.
It had a clarinet solo, and a trombone solo and a trumpet solo.
And it was your trumpet solo?
Yeah. I think it was.
Yeah. I believe it was, too. I think it was, too.
Yeah.
Who played the clarinet solo? Was it
Harry? Harry or Barney.
Oh, Barney. Barney.
Barney.
Yeah, it was Barney, wasn't it. Yeah. I mean, while Barney was in the band, nobody else played any clarinet solos, I don't think.
No.

No. I don't believe so. Well, -- well, now, see Cootie, the band was already changing character then, because in May, 1932, it was "Drop Me Off At Harlem", and "Stormy Weather". Well, you know, it had become more -- it was no longer the small band with just those few pieces, you know. It must have -- well, I don't know when it began being complete sections. But I guess probably a year or so after you joined. You must have kept adding men, huh?
Yeah. Because I think we started to going out doing theaters.
Yeah.
Around '31 or something like that.
Well, when you joined, there were three trumpets then, weren't there?
Yeah. There were three trumpets.
Because there was Artie and --
And Freddie Jenkins.
Yeah.
And myself.

Well, listen, along the lines of talking about different musicians that you worked with and so on, so let's talk about some of them while their names come up and while you were working with them. What would you say about Artie? I know you're going to say he had a beautiful tone.
Yeah. Well, he had a beautiful tone. That's one thing I could say about him. He had a real beautiful tone.
He didn't have a strong tone.
No.
He didn't have a lot of power, did he?
No. But a beautiful tone.
Well, was Artie playing the first parts all the time?
Yeah. He played a lot of the first parts. Well, I'll tell you, Duke switched parts around.
That's what I thought.
Yeah. On one number, sometimes I'd be playing second, I'd be playing first, and like that, on the same tune.
Yeah.
He'd switch the parts around.
Switch the parts around. What happened
No. That's the way he would write it.
Oh, he would write it that way.
Yeah.

I see. Well, for instance -- because on any of those numbers where the band was really -- where the brass section was really blowing out, all out, and the band was driving, I mean, Artie couldn't have played those.
No. He would give it to me.
Yeah. He'd give it to you. Well, now Posey never played a first part, ever, did he?
Very seldom.
No. Freddie Jenkins. Well, really, Freddie -- he just brought Freddie in for a little color here or there, didn't he?
But he could play.
Could he?
Yeah.
Could he really?
Yeah. He had a peculiar style, but he could play.
Well, what kind of a style did he have?
I don't know. I don't know how to explain it, but he had a peculiar style. He could play.
You mean it wasn't a straightforward thing. It was more of like an acquired -- like an olive, or something?
I think you should have records with him playing on it.
Yeah, I have. I'm just trying to get the words out of you. I know -- I do know how he sounded. Well, of course, one thing was he wasn't real powerful, Cootie.
No.
But he could improvise, though, couldn't he?
Yeah.
Yeah. He could improvise, which after all is the crux of the thing.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And he was a very good section man.
Was he?
Yeah. A very good section man.
Why? In what way?
About getting things together and blending in with the section.
Oh. Good. When you're talking about blending in, is it a matter also of tone? Is it a matter of intending your tone to blend?
Yeah. It's a matter of staying under the lead, and blending in with the lead, and blending in with the second.
Yeah. Not overshadowing where you're not supposed to.
Yeah.

Yeah. And then, so really when you talk about the phraseology of the section, according to number, if it was one of those pretty things, "Blues No More", or whatever. I can't remember right now. Or "The Saddest Tale", maybe. Some of those pretty things. Then Artie established the phraseology. He established the style --
Yeah.

-- that was coming out of the trumpet section. And you heard him, so he established the sound as well, so you got the color of the number, came out of Artie, really, didn't it. But on all numbers other than those, the phrasing, the attack, and the beat of the thing, had to come out of you.
Well, yeah.
I guess.
Well, yeah. Well, I would be playing --
The first.
The lead, yeah.
Yeah.
They would follow me.
Yeah.
And that's the only time -- I will say this -- when I was there -- that's the only time that that was noticed. And you had two other guys would cooperate and do that.
Ah. That's it.
The whole time I was in the band.
So in the trumpet sections that you played in in that band --
Yeah.
-- only that first, earliest section that you played with, that's the only section where they tried to play like one man.
Yeah. That's the only time.
Tried to be a completely unified section.
The only time. That's right.
Well, Cootie, that's partly because everybody was in love with the band. Involved with the band.
Uh-huh.
Inside themselves, everybody knew what it should be. What it should sound like and should be. Right?
That's right, yeah.
And there wasn't really rivalry there.
No.
Everybody was -- the band came first, in other words.
Yeah.
And then you mean as other additions were made, or other changes were made, you got personalities in there.
Yeah.
And as such personalities were felt and heard.
Well, as changes came along, different guys resent you telling them anything.
Yeah.
And so that's the way it went. You'd let a guy set up there. You wouldn't open your mouth to him. Let him play what he wanted to play.
Well, I'll be darned.
But before --
So nobody in the section would be in command of the section?
Well, yeah. In a way of speaking.
Yeah.

There was always arguments when Cat was there. He was supposed to be in command, and they'd have fights and things, you know, and arguments. But they didn't have that in the days when I'm speaking of.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah. And I guess that same was true of the reed section, I guess.
Yeah. They were worse.
(Laughter)
They were worse?
Yeah.
Well, of course -- I mean, when I think of it -- I haven't thought of it before, but Toby was really the first saxophone, and he was no guy to throw his weight around.
No.
Or lead or dominate a section.
They didn't have no arguments in --
In those days.
No. In those days.
No.

In the later days. Because a guy would come in the saxophone section, a new man come in there, and he'd just be setting there. A guy wouldn't tell him what he'd be playing next or nothing. He'd just be sitting there. He'd be lost. By the time he'd be getting into the number, he'd be looking for the music, we done finished.
(Laughter)
(Laughter)
Well, would you mind telling me why nobody ever helped the new guy?
No, they never helped him.
Well, why is that?
Well, I don't know. The -- they never felt like it was their duty.
(Unintelligible) An intruder or something?
