that must have been with Duke's blessing, then. Huh?
Yeah.
How did that happen? How -- you'd think that Duke felt, well, if he was going to go out on his own, well, then he was going to, and so he wished him well?
Yeah. Duke was very nice about that. Things like that. You know. He did the same thing with me.
Yeah. Tell me about what he did with you. How he did it.

Well, the first time I was contacted by Goodman, I told him about it. I told Duke about it. And we used to go out and talk, talk about it, so he would tell me what to tell him the next time he called. And he set up the deal for me.
(Laughter)

And we used to go out at night. And he said, 'Well, go ahead on. You've got a chance to make some money. And make a name for yourself.' And I left. And I said, 'Well, I'll be back in a year, after the contract is over with.' After the contract was up, I contacted him and I said, 'I'm ready for my job. The year's up.' He said, 'Oh, no, you're too big now. You can make a whole lot of money.' He said, 'Go ahead on.' He said, 'I don't need you right now.' 'Time I need you, I'll let you know.'
How about that. That's really -- I mean
there's few bandleaders would let guys who are the main guys in their band, just see them bow out, or help them to bow out, are there?

Yeah. But -- but he was nice in things like that. He did the same thing for Johnny, as you said. He gave him Billy Strayhorn, to go along with him and help him along. And after Johnny's thing was over, Johnny came on back and Billy Strayhorn came on back. They had a deal together there.
Well, did he put any money in it?
Uh-uh. They didn't need any money in it.
Oh.
He didn't need to put any money in it.

Well, it's really extraordinary that anybody would do that. It's really amazing. I mean, you don't -- in the business world, you would never find a guy at the head of a firm, and take one or two of his main men and say, 'Yeah, with my blessing, you go and start your own firm.' You know?
But I don't think -- it didn't hurt him. It wouldn't hurt him.
Well, it hurt him to lose you, Cootie, --
No.
-- and it hurt him to lose Johnny -- yes,
well, you know it did.
I don't think so.
Why do you say that?
I just don't think so, it hurt him.
It didn't hurt him at all to lose me.
Well, Cootie --
Or Johnny.
Well, Cootie, in this sense it didn't, I mean, that he was certainly big enough, and he was talented enough to be able to fix it so that the loss didn't show.
Yes.

Or didn't flag him. But -- but you know, I mean, the fact is that -- I don't suppose -- I mean, we talk about people being at their peak. You talk about Louis being at his peak with Les Hite. Well, I don't suppose the Ellington band was ever so perfect as when Cootie and Johnny were in that band, before they ever left. I think that must have been -- that was a peak. There's no question of that. Everything has its time, doesn't it?
Yeah.
I guess it --
But, in a situation like that, it didn't hurt to.
No. Well, I didn't mean, you know --
No.
I didn't mean that you were harming him.
He was glad.
No. No, it didn't.
It didn't hurt him at all.
And probably one of the things, too, is that he was always so adventurous, that the challenge of producing something different there --
Yeah.
-- to have it come up different.
Yeah.
But he didn't -- you know, that was a challenge to him, that he enjoyed coping with that challenge, didn't he?
And I thought the band sounded very, very good. Without me and Johnny Hodges.
(Laughter)
Well, listen --
I thought the band sounded wonderful.

Well, -- well, let's just see about that. Now, just a second. One minute. Because you went with Benny for one -- I'll go back to that, because I want you to tell me about that very much. But the thing is, in 1940 -- so -- I wonder when Ben went with the band. Was Ben with the band? Yes.
Yeah, Ben must have been.
Yeah. Ben Webster must have been with the band when you were there.
Yes.
So -- well, all right, let's see. You went out of the band.
Yeah.
Rex was already in the band.
Yeah.
There was you, Rex and some first trumpet player.
Wallace Jones.
Yeah. Wallace Jones. So when you went out, he got Ray?
Yeah. Ray took my place.

He got Ray. Well, that's funny. I don't -- I didn't take down any more of those titles after I got to 1940, because I knew that's what we wanted to talk about then. Well, I tell you what though, I remember, because that was just coming up before the war.
But the time I'm speaking of, Helen, --
When?
When he had Louis Bellson and what's the alto player's name?
Willie Smith?
Willie Smith.
Oh, Yeah.
In the band.
Oh, yeah.
That period of time when he was recording. He made some recordings.
Yeah.
The band sounded wonderful.
Yeah.
It was a different sounding band.
Yes, it was a different sounding band, that's true. Because Louie made a very different sound in the band, too.
Yeah.
Cootie, incidentally, on that subject, did -- did -- had Sonny -- did Sonny leave after you two left, or -- I can't remember what happened there. Do you? Sonny was still with the band when you left.
Yeah. Everybody was there.
Yeah. You left.
When I left.
Then Johnny left not too long after, was it?
No. Was it Johnny? I done forgot it.
Yeah. But I mean, I never did know -- did Sonny just -- or did Sonny fall sick or something?
Maybe Sonny was taken sick or something.
Yeah. And was Sonny replaced by Louis Bellson, or was he replaced by somebody else?
I don't know. I was gone.

I don't remember. Yeah. But -- but the sessions I remember -- well, the band, you know, reached many peaks, but one of the peaks was right then, just before you left, when they made "Perdido", "KoKo", and those things that Ben Webster contributed a tremendous amount to. In the band. Remember around that time?
Yeah.
When you were there?
Yeah, I was there.
You were there. I guess -- well, as a matter of fact, I guess it was the last session you made before you left. I believe.
Yeah, the last session -- no. The last session I made was "Concerto for Cootie". I remember that.
Yeah. Yeah. That's what we said, in 1940. As a matter of fact, I don't think Ben remained for a very much longer time after that, I don't believe.
I don't recall.
No.
Who was the next one to leave after that.
No.
I think it was Barney Bigard?
Oh, yes. Oh, yeah. Was Barney still in the band when you left?
Yeah.
Oh. Yeah, I guess that was Barney, then. Well, you know -- well, one thing, you see, the band stayed almost intact for like ten years. And then, when you went, you know --

Okay, Cootie, now we get to -- we're up to 1940 here, and we started talking about Duke when Benny got in touch with you. So I'm interested in all this. First of all, do you remember how Benny got in touch with you? Who did he go through?
Oh, I think he went through his brother.
Harry.
Yeah.
Harry Goodman, the bass player.
No. The trumpet player.
Freddie.
No, not Freddie. The other one.
Oh, Irving.
Irving.
Oh, is that right.
Yeah.
Is that right.
Uh-huh.
He got Irving to approach you, huh?
Yeah. Irving. But I liked the band. that was the main thing. (Unintelligible) A The band had a terrific beat.
Yeah.
The band sounded good.
Well, when did you hear the band? On records?
On the radio.
Yeah.
And different things.
Yeah.
The band had a terrific beat.
Oh, Gene Krupa was on drums, and --
No, Gene wasn't there then.
Davey Tough?
I think -- yeah, Davey Tough was.
Well, Davey was a very good drummer, wasn't he?
Davey Tough. Yeah. He had a terrific
rhythm.
Yeah.
And I just liked the band.
Yeah.
I liked the sound of the band.
Yeah. And you liked what Goodman was laying down, didn't you?
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
I liked -- I liked -- he could play, you know. And that's the reason why.
Yeah. Because, that's -- I mean, that band was jumping, wasn't it? And --
Yeah.
I mean, they came on the scene with something that was something else, wasn't it?
It really was.
Well, that was -- so, when you joined the band, I think they were in New York, weren't they?
I think so, yeah.

So what -- well, you were now -- well, we needn't pull any punches on this. We know -- I mean, I know Benny well, so Benny wasn't -- it started off he didn't want to offer you too much money to start with, I'm sure.
That's right.
Yeah.
So Duke would tell me --
What to tell him?
Yeah, what to tell him. No, that wasn't enough.
Yeah.
So he got to figuring what he thought it was okay, and he said, "Well, tell him okay."
Yeah. So you joined the band in New York?
Yeah.
And you sat up there in the trumpet section.
No.
Oh. You were there for the sextet.
Duke told me, "Only for the sextet." He said, "You'll get lost, sitting back there in the band."
You'll be buried.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So rig up the thing where you'll only be featured with the sextet.
Yeah.
So he drew up the contract where I was only to be featured with the sextet. Duke thought of that.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, so Georgie All was in there.
Yeah.
And Lionel.
No. Lionel wasn't there. Charlie Christian.
Oh.
Myself and Bennie. Who else was in --
Was that before? No Lionel had left, hadn't he?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And --
Who was playing piano? Not Jess. Teddy.
No. Teddy wasn't there then.
Oh, it was one of those boys --
Who was it? Powell?
Yes. Mel Powell, wasn't it?
Mel Powell.
Yeah.
Yeah. Mel Powell was there.
Yeah.
So --
And Davey.
Yeah.
And was there a bass player?
Yeah. Bernstein.
Oh, yeah. Artie Bernstein, yeah.
Yeah. Well, I'll tell you Helen, to tell you the truth, that was the most relaxed thing that I ever had in my life in music. In job or anything I ever had in music. That year.
Well, how come? I mean, you were getting a kick out of it.

Well, yeah. I enjoyed playing. I enjoyed playing. Everybody in the sextet was great. And each man that you had to follow to play behind, you had to play. And that sextet used to romp. And there wasn't no slack there.
There was nothing wrong.
Nothing wrong. At all. And you had to play. And I just enjoyed it so much.
And Benny was an inspiration.
Yeah. He played.
Yeah.
And he had to play, too.
Yeah. Yeah. Which thrilled him, because he never -- he very seldom ever had to play.
Yeah. And I just really enjoyed it, you know. And I didn't have to worry about the money or working.
Yeah.
It was the most money I had made in my life.
(Laughter)
Yeah. Yeah. And no worries.
And no worries.
Yeah.
You got a check every week. And I had never been used to that.
Yeah.
(Laughter)
Well, Cootie, the only thing was, you didn't get to play very much, though.
Yeah.
What'd you play? Three times a night? Or more?
Sometimes more. When he felt -- sometimes he kept the band off. He'd start off with the band, and then -- Friday nights, sometimes, he'd keep the sextet on.
Oh, really?
Yeah. Sometimes that sextet would stay on an hour and a half.
Oh, really?
Yeah.
Oh, well, yeah. Well, in that case, you did get enough to blow, then.
Then, sometimes, if the trumpet player wasn't there, the snag used to come in. He wanted me to set in the band.
Yeah.
And play. And sometimes I'd do it, you know.
I saw you up in the section. I caught the band one time, when you were sitting up there in the section. Yeah. Well, did you actually enjoy playing a few numbers with the band itself?
Well, yeah. I did.
Fair. Pretty fair.
No, no, I enjoyed it. Enjoyed playing too with the band, But I remembered what Duke said. "Don't let him set you up there in the band."
Yeah.
(Laughter)
And so you knew you weren't doing the right thing.
Yeah.
Yeah.
But I enjoyed it.
Yeah.
Because he had all good men in the band.
Yeah.
And he rehearsed the band. And I mean, that band played. Wasn't no way any man could do what he wanted to do and this and that.
No.
No. It wasn't going down like that.
No. Everybody was doing exactly what Goodman said.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And when that band hit, they hit.
Yeah. Yeah, there was discipline.
Yeah.
And you weren't used to that.
Yeah, in a way I was. I always disciplined myself.
I know you did.
Because I was never late. I played with Ellington, what was it, 12 years, something like that? 10, 12 years. Never was late.
Really?
Never was late. And I was accustomed to those type of things.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.
And it didn't bother me at all. You know.
No.
And the music sounded good.
Yeah.
And everything was good.
Yeah.
And that was it.
Yeah. Did Catherine go with you when you went on the road with them?
No.
No. You maybe didn't go on the road all that much. You were probably on location quite often.
Yeah.
Yeah. Was Irving in the band?
Yeah. Irving was in the band.
Irving was in the trumpet section?
Yeah.
Irving told me one time Benny made him upset so much in the section, like he did upset people so much, that Irving says he threw his horn at the wall and smashed it up.
(Laughter)
He said it just used to break his heart.
Well, they was entirely two different men, Duke and Benny. And I learned a lot from both of them. And it was a great experience.
What all did you learn from Benny?
Well --
In the way of handling a band, you mean?
Yeah, in the way of handling the band. And -- and men, too, you know, handling the band and rehearsing the band.
Did he rehearse the band well?
Oh, yeah. Did he.
He did, huh?
Yeah.
He knew just what he wanted.
Yeah. He knew just what he wanted. The only thing that Benny did that I couldn't do was pay the men for rehearsal. I didn't have no money to pay my men for no rehearsal.
Yeah. Did he pay for rehearsal?
Yeah.
Did he?
Yeah. He'd keep the band in rehearsal for a month. Before he'd -- he'd draw them out.
Oh, I see what you mean. Yeah. Yeah. But he had everybody scared, though, Cootie.
Well --
You must have been one of the few guys in the band that was sitting up there happy. Huh?
Well, not all the time. There wasn't -- he always had to have a guy that he would pick on.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah.
And then the other guys would be free.
(Laughter)
And some nights he would come in there, he would be gay and happy and go and play and wouldn't bother nobody. And so it would be okay, you know. It wasn't all the time that the guys would be afraid.
Oh. Yeah.
And those nights, you know, then they would play good.
Well, after all, one thing about it was the band sounded good, so the guys had to be happy.
Yeah.
It never probably sounded that good anywhere else, you know.
No.
The guys that were in that band sounded
good. Yeah. Did you -- did you have any buddies or anything in the band? Anybody special that you liked at all?
Well, yeah. I mean, Irving was a good buddy.
Yeah.
And Charlie. Charlie Christian.
Yeah.
Hang out with -- there used to be a little guitar player named Mike Bryant.
Oh.
We used to hang out together. And Georgie Auld.
And Davey, I guess, huh?
No. Davey didn't hang out with us.
Why not?
But he was friendly, though. He was -- I don't know. Davey didn't hang out with us.
Was he trying to stay on the wagon?
Yeah, maybe so. Davey didn't hang out with us. I didn't drink.
Oh.
But Davey didn't hang out with us, you know.
Yeah.
But -- who else in there? All of them
Yeah.
We used to get along quite good together.
Yeah.
So --
He had a pretty first saxophone player. Hymie wasn't it?
Yeah. Hymie wasn't there, though.
Oh, wasn't he?
No.
Oh.
I forgot the first saxophone player.
I forgot, too. Yeah, well, that's good. Well, what made you think -- had you signed the year's contract, you mean?
Yeah.
I see. Did he ask you to stay on?
Well, no. I wouldn't have stayed no way. Because I had promised Duke that I would be back.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah.
And I called Duke, and told Duke my year was up and I was ready for my job back. And he said, 'No, you're too big a man now.' Said, 'You've got time to make a
whole lot of money. You get a band." And we used to talk those things over. We'd go out together. He said, "You set yourself up a band and make a whole lot of money."
Well, I mean, that took quite a lot of capital. Did you have the capital?
Well, I had money.
Yeah.
But I lost a little money in the beginning.
Well, that's to be expected, I guess.
Yeah.
Well, what did you do? Did you set up for a few weeks, to rehearse a band?
Oh, yeah. And I started the band out in Chicago, and -- at the Grand Terrace.
Well, Cootie, let's first -- first let me ask you, were you with Mo Gale, or were you with Shaw?
Not in the beginning.
Were you with Shaw?
No. I was with the William Morris Agency in the beginning.
And was Willard with the agency then?
I think so.
Yeah.
So I wasn't getting no work. Then I
had tried to scuffle this thing with my band alone.
Tried to do your own booking, you mean?
No. Tried to do my own handling my band, you know.
Oh, yeah.
So, during that period of time, you had to give up some part of your band in order to be a success.
Yeah.
So I said, 'Well, I ain't going to give up no part of my band.' And it squares me out. So that's the time I came in with Moe Gale.
Oh. Well, Cootie who were you dealing with there?
Who was I dealing with?
Yeah. You know, when they were talking to you and telling you how you had to be commercial and this, that and the other.
Not commercial.
Oh.
No. I didn't have to be commercial.
Well, what were they telling you, then?
(Unintelligible). Which I knew the business.
Yeah.
About that you had to give up part of your band. Fifty percent.
What do you mean?
Fifty percent of the band.
Oh, you mean financially.
Financially.
Oh, I see. Fifty percent?
Yeah.
Wow. How about that.
So -- who was doing it -- I think Cab. He had to give up fifty percent of his.
No kidding.
Who else? All the bands around -- Jimmy Lunsford. No, he didn't give up nothing, so they squared him out. Burned the place down where he was at.
Oh.
And everybody around. Harry James. He was stewed, then. He couldn't make it. Everybody owned him. And so I went and gave up fifty percent of my band.
You did?
Yeah.
To Moe?
Yeah.
Oh, isn't that terrible.
Well, now, let me tell you. So I wasn't doing nothing. So the next year, I think I made
You did?
Yeah.
(Laughter)
How come?
Huh?
How come? You had these hit records.
I had "Cherry Red Blues", yeah. And "Things Ain't What They Used to Be". And they didn't squeeze me out. I got in all the major theaters cross country. And I played everything.
Well, Cootie, let me get this straight now. Now, just a minute. So was this your first year with Mo Gale? Or second year with Mo Gale.
This was my first year with Mo Gale.
So he was in on fifty percent of that?
He was in on fifty percent of that. So after I'd made all this money, I go to Mo Gale and tell him, I said, "Man, I can't give you fifty percent of my earnings."
(Laughter)
So I stopped giving him fifty percent.
Well, were you tied up? Did you have a contract?
There's no contract you can make with a man to get fifty percent of your earnings. So I knew that.
Oh, good. Yeah.
And so now, I'm mighty well established see, and I'm rolling on. The next year I make $150,000.00. So I started to going down. And sure as shooting, it's a control on that business.
You mean, those are going to make money where they're going to make money.
Yeah.
And if they don't have that much percentage in it, there isn't that much work being done on it.
Right.
Well, could you see the difference in the bookings?
Oh, yeah.
Is that right.
Soon as I started giving up that fifty percent, I could see the difference in the bookings.
Well, I'll be darned. Well, at that time, the Gale Agency had Ella.
Yeah.
They evidently -- I don't know what kind of written contract they had with Ella. They couldn't keep her that long, could they?
They had her a long time, though.
Yeah. And, oh, they had the Savoy
Sultans, or people like that.
Oh, they had a whole lot of trash in there.
Did they?
Yeah. Erskine Hawkins. He was very big then.
Yeah.
Buddy Johnson.
Oh, did they have Buddy Johnson?
He was big then, too.
You know, it's a funny thing about Buddy Johnson. I mean, he never got known commercially.
No.
But the way that -- it's very funny, isn't it? It must be the same type of thing. That nobody ever really moved back of that band.
Well, he was known very well in the colored field.
Yeah.
But he never did break the white field open. Once you were identified in the white field, then you were established forever.
Yeah.
But when you were only identified in the colored field --
Yeah.
Then you dropped down, and that's it.
Yeah. Somebody missed out, though, didn't they? Somebody should have had the sense to break him out of that. Since, I mean, it was a good band, wasn't it?
Yeah.
It was a swinging band.
Yeah. And he was --
Was it a Basie type band?
In a way of speaking.
Yeah.
He had -- you know, good singers with him. And the band was good. You know. But that they couldn't break the white field open.
Yeah.
He was a good composer himself.
Was he? What did he write?
He wrote a lot of them hit things.
What kind of things.
In the colored field.
He did?
Yeah.
Is that right?
He had a whole lot of hit songs.
Is he still around?

Tell you the funny thing. Me and him had the same accountant. I happened to be down in the accountant's office and he happened to call up, from Miami, Florida. He lives in Miami, Florida now. And the accountant told him that I was in the office. And put him on the phone, and he started to talking, and he was so happy to talk to me. I was happy to talk to him. Because I hadn't seen him or heard from him in years.
Yeah.
He stopped playing.
He stopped playing?
Yeah. He's a minister now.
Oh, is he really?
Yeah.
Fancy that. What was his instrument, anyway?
Piano.
Oh, it was.
Yeah. He played good piano, too.
I'll be darned. And he never even got to record, did he?
Yeah. What do you mean?
Oh, did he?
Oh, yeah.
I didn't know that.
He made thousands of records.
No kidding.
All at the price I had.
Really?
Yeah. And Sister Ella Johnson.
Really? For heaven's sake. Well, I'll be darned. Well, that was nice, wasn't it?
Yeah.
And he's a minister now. How about that.
Uh-huh.
Well, anyway, let's go back to -- to -- so, this second year you could see that bookings were a little different.
Yeah.
Did you say anything?
Well, yeah, I did say something, but that didn't mean nothing. Said they couldn't help it.
Yeah. They just played dumb.
Yeah. So then I changed offices and all. (Unintelligible). Another agency sprung up. And I went with them.
Who?
It was the Ben Bart Agency.
Oh, yeah. Universal.
Universal.
Yeah.

I went with them. And they were strictly colored, you know. Dinah Washington, I think they had. And it didn't do no good. In fact, things started to dropping. And eventually, I got the house band at the Savoy. I had the house band in the Savoy until they closed it down.
Well, Cootie, the Gale Agency wasn't going to give you the house band in the Savoy unless you were back with them, were they?
No, I had the house band in the Savoy.
Well, were you being handled by them?
Yeah. No, I wasn't handled by them then. I tell you, I was working in the Savoy all the time, you know, with the Gale Agency.
Yeah.
I had built up a big reputation at the Savoy Ballroom.
Yeah.
So they needed me up there.
Yeah. They had to have a band that could draw and that could mean something.
Yeah. And produce.
Yeah.
And I had that type of band. So they cut my band down to seven pieces. Okay, cut it down to seven
pieces. Things was bad there. Then I stayed there till they tore it down, with seven pieces.
Who were those seven pieces?
Oh, I had an organ, a rhythm section, myself --
You didn't have Kenny Kersey, did you?
No.
You had him earlier, though, didn't you?
Yeah.
We'll go back to that in a minute.
And -- who did I have on tenor? The tenor player -- and Rupert Cole, alto.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh. We had a trombone player.
Could Rupert Cole -- did he solo?
Not particularly, no.
No. But you needed him there for your arrangements and things.
Yeah.
Yeah. Who did you say you had on tenor?
I'm trying to think. Can't think of the tenor player.
It wasn't Lockjaw?
No, no. It wasn't Lockjaw then.
Well, we'll go back to that. Or we'll ask
Stan if we have to.
Yeah.
Well --
George Clark.
Oh. Oh, I see. Who was your drummer?
Who was my drummer then? Les Jenkins.
Oh. I see. But that lasted about seven years.
Yeah. I stayed there.
We'll retrace our steps for dates, because what we didn't go into yet, which we should, is like, you know, when you got Cleanhead, and so on.
Yeah.
So, let's go back to when you were rehearsing your band.
Yeah.
I mean, were you pretty excited? The idea that you were going to have your own band, and you were picking your guys, and you were rehearsing?
Well, yeah.
Or were you a little nervous about it?
No, I wasn't nervous about it. John Hammond was helping me in a little way. Not -- in the way that he had. Financially, too. I went to -- down in Texas to get a tenor player.
Arnett Arnie Cobb?
Arnett Arnie Cobb.
Yeah.
But he was working with a band called Larkins Milton Lockett, and they were working a roadhouse. And he was an insurance man in the daytime.
Oh.
So his wife wouldn't let him leave.
Oh.
So I couldn't get him. So I went through all this money to go down in Texas.
Oh. You mean, you just went down personally? Yourself?
Yeah.
No kidding.
Yeah. To get him.
Well, I never.
So, See, John Hammond wanted me to go down there and get him.
Yeah.

So, I'm out there listening to the band at this roadhouse. They split up the band. I'm in the kitchen. And Cleanhair got up and started to singing. He wasn't singing with the band. He started to singing the blues. I come out of that kitchen and run right down front. I said,
"This is what I want."
(Laughter)
And that's how I found Cleanhead.
But he told me, or you told me, or somebody told me, that he couldn't take you seriously.
I'm telling you, he wasn't singing with the band. He was kidding and joking around.
With that falsetto and all that?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And that was what I wanted. And I heard him singing them blues. I -- and I told him I wanted him. I offered him this money, and I stuck with him.
Well, didn't you have a hard time? Because he had his dad there, in Houston, didn't he?
Yeah.
You had a hard time getting him away, didn't you?

No, not him. I eventually got him to New York. Eventually -- I had the band, all my band, picked. And I had called rehearsal. So I had to go down to the station to meet him. I had sent for him to come here. So he came in on the train. And he didn't have no case with his horn. Had this old silver horn under his arm. I said, "No, I can't take him into rehearsal like this, and this bald head." (Unintelligible.)
(Laughter)
So I had to stop him down at my manager's and get him a horn with a case.
No kidding.
