Lockjaw's from Texas.
Yeah.
I mean, I don't think he -- he hadn't been playing with a lot of people then, had he? Or had he?
No, he hadn't.
No.
I'm the first big band he played with.
Oh, you are.
Yeah.
Well, Lockjaw wasn't so schooled on reading. Am I right?
Yeah. He made it all right with me.
Did he?
Yeah. Because during that period of time, if a guy had a little talent, I would take time for him to learn how to read. And to bring it out of him.
How would you do that?
By rehearsing him.
Oh.

And teaching him. That's a good way. That's a part of -- Benny didn't teach anyone, but he schooled the guys that he hired. They knew how to read, but they didn't know how to phrase or anything, and I could picture myself setting there in front of the band, picture Benny setting there in front of the band, stopping them and telling them what to do. And I did the same thing.
You did. Sing it for them.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And that's the reason I took it. I learned a lot from Goodman, you know.
Yeah.
And Duke.
Yeah. Well, did any of these guys ever tell you thank you, later?
Oh, yeah.
Really?
Yeah. A lot of them thanked me.
No kidding?
Uh-huh.
Well, you had a happy band, I take it.
Oh, yeah.
On the whole, I take it.

Yeah. Well, I was very good in finding talent and bringing it out of them. It was in the rough and raw. But I would work with it very hard. In later years I stopped doing it, because my patience wasn't so good.
Yeah. Time takes its toll, doesn't it?
Yeah.

Yeah. Well, one thing I didn't -- I didn't ask you about -- I'll go back. There's a few more guys here I want to talk -- well, maybe I'd better talk about the guys first, and then ask you what I want. Where'd you find Emmett Berry?
I don't know. Emmett Berry. I can't place any Berry being there.
In your band?
No.
Oh.
That's something I can't place.
Well, you know, these books make a mistake, sometimes. Now, they said that -- they said Money Johnson was in your band.
Yeah. Money Johnson.
But, no. You didn't have Emmett? Huh?
I can't --
Maybe he just made a record with you or something.
Yeah. But I can't place --
Well, just on the subject of Emmett, because I might forget, he's a nice trumpet player, isn't he?
Yeah. A real nice trumpet player.
Yeah. Who did you hear him with?
Emmett Berry?
Yeah. I guess he was with Fletcher, wasn't he? Or -- who was --
I can't place ---
-- Berry with?
Who was Emmett Berry with?
(Laughter)
That's funny. He was blowing so much at one time, wasn't he? He was making an awful lot of record sessions.
Yeah.
But what band was he with?
He wasn't with Fats, was he?
No. I don't think so. And he wasn't -- it wasn't Basie. I have a feeling he was with Fletcher. Smack. I think he was. In the later years, you know.
Yeah.
I believe that's where he was maybe.
Yeah, maybe.
Well, then, where did you find Money
Money Johnson? Where did I find Money Johnson? I can't recall.
I'm going to switch off a minute here.

Cootie, something that I didn't talk to you about. We've talked about all that time you were with Duke, and you never drank anything on the job, and so on. Oh, you never drank anything. And even with Goodman, you never drank anything. Well then, so, you got your own band together. What happened to you? You not only developed a taste for scotch, but was it a difference in your outlook, or what was it as well?
I don't know. Maybe handling men and seeing their reaction and going out on parties, with people inviting you out, and the thing that I never did drink. So I started to drinking.
Well, you mean in a way you were being like feted and everything. You were the star, really.

Yeah. And being, you know, invited out to different places, and I started to drinking. I'd have a drink here, a drink there and a drink there. So I acquired a taste for scotch. And so I started to hitting it. But --
Well, did this develop over two or three years, or something, you know, when you first had the band? Or
Oh, about two years after I had the band, I imagine.
Yeah.
But I never did drink steady. If I would drink two or three months, I would lay off two or three months.
Really?
Yeah.
Well, what would bring you to lay off?
I don't know.
-- that you were doing the wrong thing for yourself?
Yeah. Uh-huh. And check myself out. If I would drink this year, the next year I wouldn't drink.
No kidding.
Yeah.

Well, I know one thing that you said to me before somewhere, that drinking or smoking pot and so on, that you could labor under the delusion that you're helping your -- what you're playing and everything. But that this is an illusion. That it's not true.
No.
You're probably hurting what you're doing.

Yeah. And I found out that it makes you nervous. It works on the nervous system. I don't think you have the horn, the instrument under control, when -- when you're not drinking, I used to always have my instrument under control. And I found out that wasn't no good.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.
And that's the reason why I used to check myself, drink two or three months and lay off.
No kidding.
Yeah.

Well, besides that, there's the fact that if you're drinking, and if you're being entertained, and you're the star or whatever, and you're drinking, even if you don't know it at the time, you know it the next day, that maybe everything wasn't just exactly the way you wanted it to be, because as you say, you're not really in control. If you're drinking, you don't know exactly just, you know, you're maybe not acting just the way you would be doing if you weren't drinking.
That's correct. I don't see where alcohol ever helped anyone, unless they were sick.
Yeah.
And I've been around many persons that drank and drank and drank, and it half killed a lot of good

musicians. Famous musicians, alcohol has. And I see this thing has happened to them. And maybe, yes, when I look at them, and I see them, that's the reason I don't drink today, again. It's been about 18 years since I had a drink of alcohol.
18 years?
Uh-huh.
Has it really? No kidding. So back, like in '58 or something.
Yeah.
About the time that you began to have the small band? Am I right?
Yeah.
Were you still drinking when you had the seven pieces?
I think that's when I stopped drinking, I think.
Is it?
Yeah.
Of course, you were doing more blowing then, Cootie. If you were only seven pieces.
Yeah.
Am I right? You had -- I mean you had to be --
No, I was blowing a lot with the big band, too.
Oh. Because you were playing parts too, weren't you?
Not particular parts. Because the thing was built around me.
Yeah.
All the arrangements that were brought in..
Yeah.
The arranger would build the thing around me.
Yeah.
I had to blow.
Yeah.
All the time.

Yeah. I know, of course, one thing is that's one way that you have the respect of your musicians, too, you know. If you are blowing all the time, and things are built around you and you're delivering. I mean, that's when you're entitled to look to everybody else to deliver, when you yourself are delivering.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. Everyone should be able to deliver when they're playing music. It's not no one man job.
Yeah.
You've got a band, you've got 14 or 15 men, all of them are supposed to deliver.
Yah. But quite often, in the case of a leader, a leader sometimes supplies something else, and he's not delivering on an instrument the same way.
I said what Duke used to say. He said, 'I'm no good without the band.'
Yeah.
And I used to tell him the band is no good without him.
Yeah.
Because usually, if Duke wasn't there, that band was nothing.
Yeah. Yeah.
Just his appearance and calling the tunes, and things, made a whole world of difference.
Yeah. The fact that he was there.
Yeah.
And the boss was there.
Yeah.
And you didn't fool around.
It's not the matter of not fooling around. It's just that the whole thing changed.
Yeah. Well, in other words, he was an inspiration.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, listen, Cootie, if there's

not anything comes to your mind, anything particularly significant, during those years when you had the big band, well then, in, let's see, we said '42 to '55, I think you had the big band. And then from '55 to '62, you had the seven pieces at the Savoy. Did you go out at all from there, with the seven pieces?
Very seldom.
Yeah. You were mostly there.
Yeah.
And was that in any way due to Charlie Buchanan, the Savoy? Or was that strictly, as far as -- or simply that Moe Gale just hired you.
No, not Moe Gale. Charlie Buchanan. He was the manager.
The manager of your band?
No. The manager of the Savoy.
The manager of the Savoy, yeah. So you mean Charlie hired you.
Yeah.
Oh. Well, why was I always under the impression that the Savoy was physically or financially tied up with the Gale agency too? Were Charlie and Moe partners in some way?
Yeah.
Yeah. They weren't equal partners?
No. I think --
Well, Charlie probably started off in a small way, and got bigger.
Yeah. And got bigger, yeah.
Yeah. One --

But the main reason why they kept me there, Helen, not because I was Cootie Williams, a jazz player. It was because I produced. They used to have certain nights for certain types of music. And I learned to play that type of music. They used to have on Wednesday nights, club nights, where they would have the older people there. And I learned how to play the waltzes and the slow music. On Monday nights and Thursday nights, that was jitterbug night. I had to learn to play their type of music. So they wanted me, the jitterbugs. And the older crowd that come there, they wanted me. And on Sunday afternoon, they would have matinees, club dances, and I used to learn how to play club music for that type of thing. So I was well rounded, with all types of music to play for the types of people that came to the Savoy Ballroom.
Yeah. Yeah.
So that's the main reason why Charlie Buchanan kept me there.
Yeah. Yeah. Because you filled the bill.
Yeah.
Everybody's bill. Yeah. I see. Well,
you wouldn't -- you didn't have too much trouble with the guys, then, because you were on location. I mean, everybody likes to stay in town.
Yeah. Everybody likes to stay in town.
Let's -- we said -- you couldn't -- you weren't so sure who were those seven pieces you had then. Let's think back. Did you say -- was Sam Taylor with you then?
No. Sam Taylor wasn't there. I think I told you who was there.
Oh, you said Rupert Cole.
Rupert Cole. And who else was there?
Your drummer -- uh, you told me who the drummer was. Well --
I had an organ player. His name was Preston. Fabulous Preston, we used to call him.
(Laughter)
He could swing.
Could he?
Yeah. I had about three different organ players, you know, during the period of time I was in there.
Yeah.
With the seven pieces. And George -- who did I say? George -- what was his name? The tenor player.
Oh, yeah. You did tell me. Well -- I don't know why it's gone out of my mind.
He was the tenor player.
Yeah. We have got it on the tape, because you did say who it was.
Yeah. We have got it on the tape.
Well, listen, so that -- you were satisfied to have an organ, because I suppose under those circumstances, too, it filled a bill, too, didn't it?
Yeah.
I mean --
Well, that's what he wanted.
Oh.
He wanted an organ group.
Yeah.
So I picked up an organ group for him.
Yeah. Yeah. Right.
And it turned out to be successful and I learned how to blend the three horns together with the organ, and it sounded like a big band.
Yeah, of course, because you got section sounds out of the organ, then.
And with the three horns together, too.
Yeah.
You got another voice from the horns.
You got a big sound with the organ. So it'd make it sound like a big band.
Yeah. That's something I didn't ask you about. Who was writing for you during these years?
Oh, I had many writers.

Well, I mean like with the first band, with the big band in the beginning. What kind of writers did you pick on, in the very beginning, when you started rehearsing? Did you -- Buster Harding or people like that?
No.
Who, then? Can you remember?
Well, I had three vocalists in the band.
Yeah.
And all three of them was different.
Yeah.
And I had three different writers.
Yeah.
Don Redman used to do things for Pearl Bailey.
Oh, did he?
And Don Kirkpatrick --
Oh, yeah.
-- used to do things for Eddie Vinson. He did all of Eddie Vinson's things.
Oh, yeah.
And the ballad things, I used to have a white boy do all the ballads.
What was his name? Can you remember?
I can't remember off hand who he was.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I see.
And then some of the swing things, I would get different swing arrangers.
Yeah.
To do the --
Yeah. People that you knew, and people that you --
Yeah.
-- that would come in and ask you if they could do things for you, too, I guess.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, then, when you had the seven pieces, did you write some of the things?
No. Not all of them, but some of them.
Yeah.
But the majority of all the things, I would get an arranger, and have him to come and listen. Before he would make arrangements for me, he would have to come and listen, to see what I was doing.
Yeah.
Before he would make arrangements.
To see what you wanted.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Before he could make arrangements for me.
In that time, Cootie, who was doing any vocals for you then? With the seven pieces.
Oh, we had a guitar player. What was his name? And a blues singer, too. He played the guitar. I'll think of his name after awhile.
All right. Funny, I'm not sure. You don't know who he worked with --
Larry Pale.
Oh, I see. Was he a good guitar player?
Yeah. He was a country guitar player.
Oh.
Played that country guitar and sang country blues.
Yeah. Well, I know something else that we haven't said. In what numbers were you singing with your own band?
None at all. I don't like my singing.
Oh, surely.
Uh-uh.
Cootie. All the numbers you sang with Duke, and you didn't sing any with your own band?
No. I don't like my singing.

Well, that's funny you should say that, because you know what you said about Pearl, that an artist often doesn't know what they can do. Well, I mean the point is maybe you wouldn't consider yourself that you're a singer, because of course you're a trumpet player and not a singer. But what you had to offer was something -- it was something that pleased. It was funny, it was -- you brought something to it. And well, I liked it very much.
I'll tell you a funny thing.
A lot of people did.

I'll tell you a funny thing. When I was out doing a single, I was up in Toronto, at one of the nightclubs up there, one of the spots up there, doing a single, and I had to learn about four songs. And the public, that's all they wanted me to do, was sing.
Isn't that funny.
And I would tell them I didn't know no more songs. I was a trumpet player. I wasn't no singer.
(Laughter)
"Come on, Cootie, sing. Sing. Sing."
Isn't that funny?
And today, being an entertainer, a
jazz trumpet player, it's very hard. Just to be a jazz trumpet player.
Yeah.
You have to be an entertainer. On top of it, entertaining, telling jokes.
Yeah.
Dancing around.
Yeah.
Sing.
Sell yourself.
Yeah.
Yes.
That's the business today.
Yeah.
Not only blowing that trumpet. Don't care how much trumpet I can blow, they want me to entertain them, singing and dancing, and telling jokes.
Yeah.
Now, that's the business today. I found that out doing a single. That's one thing I wanted to say.
Yeah. Like, you mean, after the Savoy closed down.
Yeah.
Yeah. And did what, the Gale Agency send
As a single, yeah.
And this is all they wanted from you, all this?
Yeah.
Well, did you have a band? Did you have a group?
No. I played with the group.
Whoever the group was, huh?
Whoever the group was, I played with the group and sang, rehearsed with them and sang with them.
And you certainly didn't like that, did you?
No. I lost about 14 pounds in one week.
Did you really?
Jumping around.
Yes. And then have to submit to bad musicianship.
That's when I came back with the band.
Yeah.
That's when I came back with Duke's band.
Yeah. I mean, was the money that good, to justify it?
Yeah, the money was good, but as you said, playing with bad musicians.
Yeah.
Sometimes the musicians couldn't read.
Yeah.
They didn't know chord structure or nothing.
Yeah.

I'd be playing, maybe, 'Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me', and they'd be playing something else. You have to learn that in this business. See, the public is very funny. You're standing in front of the public out there, they don't want to know nothing about John Doe back there.
Yeah.
Everything is on you.
Yeah.
They're listening to you. I learned how to keep blowing, regardless of what them people are doing back there.
Yeah.
And I would finish my song, and I don't know where the hell they would be at.
(Laughter)
Oh, that must be very depressing.
Yeah, it is.
Yeah.
But all that's in the business, that you have to learn.
Yeah. Yeah.
And a lot of people can't do that.
No. I know that. Well, now, wait a minute. Let's pause here a minute.

Cootie, it just would be nice to talk a minute with you about some of the guys that you worked with, and some of the guys that you knew one way or another, and just see what you might have to say. Sometimes you won't have anything to say, but for instance, well, what about Harold Baker. I know, let's take some trumpet players, because you've always got something to say about trumpet players. What about Harold? What kind of musician was Harold?
Harold Baker?
Yeah.
He was a wonderful trumpet player, but I never had the pleasure of working with him. I wasn't there.
Oh.
But I heard him on records. He was a marvelous trumpet player.
Yeah. He had a marvelous conception for a first man, didn't he?
Yeah.
And more than a first man.
Yeah. A wonderful trumpet player.
Yeah. And did a lot for the band.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, another guy that was a nice trumpet player, was Willie Cook.
Yeah. Willie Cook was a real nice trumpet player.
He's got a very individual kind of conception. Don't you think he has? I think his style is based on Louis, really, isn't it? Would you say?
In a way, yeah. Uh-huh.
I guess you never worked with him, did you?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah, you did work with him.
I did work with him.
When you came back, didn't you?
Yeah.
Well, what did he offer the section? Was he a good section man?
He was a good section man.
Was he cooperative?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Where's your reservation?
Well, he wasn't nothing like Harold Baker.
No.
Not as a trumpet player, no.
Yeah. No. Clark Terry.
Oh, wonderful.
Really?
Oh, yeah.
(Laughter)
No kidding?
Yeah. Clark Terry's a wonderful trumpet player. Oh, he's terrific.
Well --
Yeah. I love him very much.
Well, tell me why.
Well, he has a great sound. And he produces. That's what I likes about him, you know, that's what I like about him. He has a great, a real great sound on his horn. And he's a very fine musician, too.
Yeah, I know that.
Yeah.
But he plays an awful lot of notes, Cootie.
But he could play the other style, too.
Yeah.
Yeah. He plays wonderful. He's a wonderful trumpet player. I think he's about one of the best trumpet players around today. Jazz trumpet players.
You do.
Yeah.
Well, do you feel that he filled a good role in that band, and do you feel that he filled as much of a role as he could have? Do you think Duke made as big a hole for him as he might have?
I don't think he had a good chance there in the band.
Why?
I don't know. I maybe figure that -- Duke maybe figured that if he left, he'd leave a big hole, so he didn't give him --
Oh, I see. So he controlled it.
Yeah.
Yeah. So he didn't have a full rein, did he?
No.
No. Well, there's some other guys. Well, tell me about Paul.
Oh, Paul was a great saxophone player. When And Paul was straight, I think he was one of the greatest tenor
saxophone players around.
You do?
Yeah. When he was straight.
Do you feel he did as much in the band as Ben did?
Yeah.
You did.
In his area, yeah.
Yeah. He was more -- something more of a modernist than Ben, wasn't he?
Yeah. He was a great musician, too, Paul.
Yeah.
When you'd catch him straight, he was something else.

Yeah. Just on that subject, because we were going to talk about how Duke did about that, so Duke was pretty canny when guys were pulling something, or when things happened to guys. I mean, when Paul would come on and he would be stoned, or something like that, or he'd be sitting up there sound asleep or something, Duke would throw his number at him, wouldn't he?
That's right. The hardest number Paul had to play, Duke would call.
(Laughter)
Everybody'd be talking about, 'No, Duke, he can't make it.' Duke would go right ahead.
(Laughter)
The fastest he could play it.
(Laughter)
Well, what was Duke's thinking on that? Would he just enjoy that? Or --
I don't know, but that's what he would do every time.

That's what he would do. He would do that to -- well, didn't he also, keeping guys on their toes, didn't he sometimes call a number, say, like, well, say, call a number that was Paul's, and Paul not be on the stand, and somebody else have to fall in there and scuffle with it?
Oh, sometimes he would, yeah.
I mean, that's --
He would have Harold Ashby play it.
Yeah.
Harold Ashby would fall right in and play it.
Yeah. What about Harold Ashby? Did you like him?
Yeah. A wonderful saxophone player.
Yeah.
Not like Paul, though.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, listen, now, let's talk about drummers just for a moment. What about Rufus in that band?
He was all right.
(Laughter)
What do you mean?
Well, that wasn't the kind of drummer you looked to hear in that band, was it?
Yeah, he was all right. He was a good drummer.
He's a good drummer, isn't he? Yeah. Okay. Yeah, well, what about Bootie Wood and Britt Woodman. What about those trombone players?
Oh, Bootie Wood's a fine trombone player.
Yeah.
I like Bootie Wood.
Yeah.
Brittman, I wasn't around him.
No. Bootie played more with the plunger than anybody else got to play after -- almost after Tricky, wouldn't you say?
I think so.
Yeah. Well, Quentin Jackson used it.
Quentin Jackson, yeah.
Yeah.
He was a very good player.
He was a good musician, wasn't he?
Yeah.

Well, I was going to ask you about some of those bass players. I was going to ask you about Pettiford and about Ernie Shepherd. But really, you sort of intimated that it was more a question of soloists, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Did you enjoy Blanton?
I enjoyed Blanton's solo work very much.
Yeah.
But I think the band was a little too heavy for Blanton. You know, as a bass player.
Yeah. Because he was young, too, wasn't he?
Yeah.
Yeah.
I told you the one I liked was Billy Taylor.
Was Billy Taylor, yeah.
Yeah.
I just want to ask you about Gus Johnson,
because I saw you had him working for you at one time. You like him as a drummer?

Yeah. Gus Johnson's a very fine drummer. According to what type you wanted him for. Gus Johnson is drumming now for singers in small groups. It's a different feeling with small groups and singers, and you fitting in with a big band.
With a big band, yeah. But he -- I mean he was a heavy enough drummer to fit in with a band. Well, that's how he started off, as a band drummer, didn't he?
Yeah.
Cootie, before we get through here, just let's talk a few minutes about you went back to the band. You sent word -- well, you went with Benny for a very -- very briefly, didn't you?
Yeah. For a year.
Oh, for a year.
Yeah.
Well, did you enjoy that?
Oh, I loved it. We talked about --
No, no. I mean, just -- you know, Benny came back from Russia --
Oh.
In 1962. You went -- I think you were
with Benny very briefly, weren't you?
Yeah. I went on a road --
A road tour?
A road tour, yes. He asked me to go on a road tour with him.
How was that? Was that a bit not just what you were looking for?
No.
No. That wasn't the same thing.
No.
A lot of years had passed by then.
Yeah.
Right. Okay. So, well, then you saw Harry, and you told him --
Yeah.
-- to tell the man.
That's right.
That I'm ready, huh? So that was that. That was just arranged right then and there, huh?
Yeah.
Well, that's nice. I'll bet Duke was awful happy.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. What did it feel like to sit back up there again? That had been -- that had been 21 years, since
you'd been in that -- no, 23 years.
Yeah.
Since you'd sat up there.
Uh-huh. It felt fine. Felt like I was back home.
Yeah. That was nice.
Yeah.
Because there was enough of the real family in it, too, to -- there was Harry and Johnny and --
Yeah.

Well, I'm just trying to think. Well, Procope and Paul. Of course you hadn't worked with Paul before. But anyway, it was still the band. Well, Cootie, right away, you made a record session which was wonderful. You made that "Afro Bossa Salsa".
Yeah.
That was nice, wasn't it?
That was real nice.
Very nice. Then he did a number for you. "Tootie for Cootie".
Yeah.
You remember?
Yeah, I remember that. Yeah.
Did he record that, do you know?
I don't know if we were recorded it or not. I think
I think so.

Oh. And then, around in the beginning there, he wrote the "New Orleans Suite". Well, I don't know, that that wasn't in the beginning at that. But he wrote the "New Orleans Suite", and he had the tribute to Louie Armstrong in there that you played.
Yeah.
Remember? That was a beautiful thing.
Yeah. Uh-huh.

Well, I wanted to ask you, before we get through, I just wanted to ask you which of his -- which of the Ellington things you really -- which ones were your favorites? So I want to just get back to that, Cootie, if you'd keep it in your mind. He did "My People" in 1963. I wanted to ask you what you feel about Jimmy Jones. He's a good musician, isn't he?
Oh, wonderful musician.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
A good accompanist, too?
Yeah.
But he's a fine arranger and a --
A fine arranger, yeah.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
I think he did "My People" for Duke. I think he did an awful lot of the scoring on it.
Yeah.

Or maybe mostly the conducting. I don't remember. But I remember he had quite a bit to do with it. In that same year, that was the first tour of the Near East and the Middle East. That must have been a little different experience.
Well --
Or was it still the same thing? Still a lot of concerts and a lot of audiences.
That's right.
Yeah.
Yeah. The same thing.
Okay. And the next year it was Japan, and Mercer had joined the band then. He joined as the band -- well, he played in a section, but he was the band manager, I guess, huh?
Yeah.
Right. Then he wrote the "Far East Suite", which was beautiful. "Mt. Harisa" and "Isfahan,"
Yeah. I remember all those things.
They were beautiful, weren't they?
Yeah. They were beautiful.
That was a nice suite. Then, in '65, well

that's when it really began, when he started the Sacred Concerts. And -- you know, I would just like to speak to you about that for a second. You know, he was working on that at Grace Cathedral, wasn't he, and the West Coast.
Uh-huh.
Well, Duke was a religious man.
Yeah.
And he always was a religious man, wasn't he?
Yeah, he was.
Yeah. So it was quite a logical thing for him to do the sacred music.
Yeah. Because he'd read the Bible through and through, many times.
Yeah. So it was something that everybody could feel for, doing the Sacred Concerts. I guess it was quite an exciting concept for everybody, wasn't it?
Yeah, it was. You know, the number that he wrote for me --
Which?
"The Shepherd".
Oh, yes. Of course.
It was a funny thing. First he was playing it on the piano. He wasn't playing it, he was just running it over. He called me down and said, "Hey, Coots, come

here." He said, "How do you like this number? Do you think you would like to play this number?" I said, "Yeah." I said, "I'll play it." So he wrote a lead sheet out on it. So I started messing around with it. He said, "What do you think of it?" I think it was about a week. I said, "Give me a chance. Give me time to feel the thing, so I can get something out of it." So we made an arrangement on it. So I started to playing it. He said, "Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah." "You're right." And that's how that number come about.
Isn't that terrific. That is wonderful. So, I mean, until you played, he didn't know what he -- he didn't have it, until you played it, really.
No.
Yeah. Then there was the number.
There was the number.
Yeah. That's wonderful. Who played that after you?
I don't think nobody.
Nobody.
No.
No. I guess he didn't play it again, did he? After he -- '73, or whatever, you know, when you stayed back, you know?
Yeah.
When it was a bad time. Well, --
Well, in '73, you know, I taken sick.

I know you did. I know you did. That's right. I want to talk about that. So let's -- I want to -- we're coming to that. So wait one second, now. Oh, yeah, Cootie, in '66, which was Dakar and Senegal, I think that must have been the Festival of the Arts, over there in Africa, because when he came back he wrote "La Plus Belle Africaine", which is a beautiful number.
Yeah.
Remember?
Uh-huh.
That's a beautiful number. Now, '67, Strayhorn died. So Strayhorn had been sick about at least a year, then, hadn't he?
Yeah.
And that's when Strayhorn sent "Blood Count" over for the band at the record session, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Yeah. That must have been very hard for Duke, wasn't it? I mean, he really minded, didn't he?
Yeah. He did. He really minded.

Another thing that Duke did to show -- which exhibited what a big man he was, was the way he gratuitously and continuously gave people credit, didn't he? And I mean, all through the years he would always speak of Billy
Strayhorn, didn't he?
Yeah.
Every performance.
That's right.
He always, continuously spoke of Billy. And I mean, that's really not what you'd expect. Not what most people do, is it?
No. Not what most people do.
No. I mean, it wasn't even as if Billy was looking for it. Because he was like Duke in that way, too. He never pushed himself forward either, did he?
No.

No. It's very remarkable. Well, Cootie, then 1968 was that second Sacred Concert at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. I just wanted to talk to you about that beautiful voice, Alice Babbs. Surely you love that voice, don't you?
Yeah. Oh, she had a wonderful voice. A terrific voice.
Don't you think that what she had was something that absolutely belonged in there with the band? That sound. Or do you?
Yeah.
I don't want to put words in your mouth.
Well, no. That's what Duke -- Duke
wrote the thing for her.
Yeah.
He had her in mind, writing it.
Yeah. So, in other words, he did for her --
Yeah.
-- like he did for the guys in the band.
So she was another Ellington voice, really.
Yeah.
Yeah. Of course, he did that with Kay Davis, too, didn't he?
Yeah.
He wrote things for Kay Davis.
Uh-huh.
But I don't think there was ever a voice that he wrote anything for that could equal hers. Do you?
Who?
Alice Babs.
No.
No. I mean, you know, there have been other singers that have done the 'Sacred Concert' since, but it's not the same thing, really is it?
No.
Well, Cootie, that same year was South America. That was fun, wasn't it? That tour.
South America?
Yeah. Don't you remember? The people rioted, just mobbed you in the streets, they were so thrilled to hear the band after all those years?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
And Stanley tells me the people were crying.
Yeah.
With joy.
Yeah.
He said that Duke and the rest of you said there hadn't been anything like that since 1933, when you first went to London.
Went to London, yeah.
I mean, that's a big thrill, isn't it. Such a long time in between. That's 35 years that had elapsed.
Yeah.
Between those two things. So that must have been quite thrilling. I see you have an award there, from Brazil. Was that at that time?
Yeah. That was at that time.
What was it, a musical society or something?
Yeah. A jazz musical society, I think.
Yeah. Well, there must have been a lot of
musicians and what not that were just thrilled to greet you.
Oh, yeah. It was.
Although, most of them did not speak English, did they?
The ones around us spoke English.
Did they?
Yeah.

Oh, that's good. That's wonderful. Well, okay, then '69 was Duke's birthday party at the White House, wasn't it? And later on in '69, Wild Bill joined the band. What would you have to say about what Wild Bill brought to the band?
Well, I don't know.
Do you think he did contribute anything, particularly, or he just filled a role that Duke had in mind.
I think he filled a role what Duke had in mind.
Yeah. 'One More Time.'
Yeah.
(Laughter)
Well, now, in '70 was another tour of the Far East. And '70, I guess, was the first real bad blow for the band, when Johnny died.
Yeah. A real bad blow.
I guess nothing was ever really quite the
same after that, was it? I mean, you know, it couldn't be quite the same after that.
No.

There's something I want to ask you about that, if -- I don't know whether you want to say or not, but Duke and Johnny had such a funny relationship. Of course I realize that for any band leader, he's always scared to death of his stars, because everything is working so that they're always going to hit them for something more. And you know, as an ex-bandleader, that there isn't all that money like guys in the band think there is. A bandleader has a lot of problems, and a lot of financial problems, right?
That's right.

And he is always scared, because a thing mushrooms and grows, and every time you have to say yes, you're scared the next time is coming up again. Right? Don't you think, in a way, that had to influence Duke's relationship with Johnny, because Johnny was one of his most important voices.
I don't think so.
Don't you?
That was a very close relationship there, between those two. Always, you know. Johnny was real close to him, you know. They was real tight.
Oh. I'm so glad to hear you say that,
because you know what a funny guy Johnny was about all -- you know how deadpan he was, and all those funny things he would say up on the stand.
It didn't mean nothing.
It didn't mean nothing. No. It was really funny, wasn't it?
Yeah.
I mean, it was Johnny's humor, wasn't it?
Yeah. (Unintelligible) -- came down to Duke, himself.

But there was one thing, though, Cootie, I mean, that is that, of course, he used to have had to keep Johnny's things toward the end, like he did yours too. But nobody ever got to hear enough of Johnny. I mean, you never got to get that one last more encore that you wanted. And don't you think that maybe Duke had to do it that way --
He played enough.
(Laughter)
He didn't play enough for anybody that wanted to hear him. Well, anyway, I'm glad to hear you say that. That's beautiful. Well, then, the last thing now, Cootie, you got sick in '73, didn't you?
Yeah.
Yeah. Right about '73. How did it come about? How did you find that out and so on? Or you just

Yeah. We was playing up at the race track. We played the matinee. I went out to play the "A Train". I come back to my seat, and they wanted me to take a bow, and I couldn't hardly get up to take a bow.
Suddenly?
Suddenly. Yeah. I had been feeling bad.
Yeah.

I said, "Something's wrong. I got to go back home. I got to go home. There's definitely something wrong with me." I had been to the doctor before we left here. And I go back to my doctor, Dr. Arthur Logan, and he take an x-ray of my lung. And we was leaving out the next day.
For where?
We were going down south.
Yeah.
Doing some one nighters. And we was down at an Army base, Camp LeJeune, I think.
Yeah.

And he says, "Well, call me back on Wednesday. Call home on Wednesday, and find out." This was on a Saturday or Sunday or something. I called home, and my wife says, "Well, Dr. Logan says you've got to come home right
Oh.
I got right out of there right away. I caught the next plane.
I'll bet you did.
And come home.
I guess that's the last thing that ever crossed your mind.
Yeah. And I wasn't going to play anymore.
Well, especially with a lung, and blowing so hard.

I had hated to give it up. No, I said, this is it. So the band went to Europe. I was only in the hospital -- how long was I in the hospital? About three or four weeks, I think. The put me right in the hospital. I had a private room. They sent me on home. But I had to take the medicine for a year.
No kidding. Did you start to feel -- get more strength then?
Yeah.
Slowly, huh?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And after I took my medicine for a year,
they took me off the medicine. I had to go back every two months. Then they started every three months, like that. Every six months. Now I go back once a year for a checkup.
Yeah. Yeah.

But during the period of time they were over there, Duke called me. He says, -- called me twice, I think. He says, "Are you ready to come back to go to work?" I said, "No, man. I ain't thinking about working no more." He said, "Ah, don't do that, man." He said, "I miss you so much." He said, "Come on back. You don't have to blow. Just sit up there and hold on."
Oh.
I said, "Okay. I'll do it for you. Nobody else in the world I would do this for but you." And that's when I went back to work with him. The doctor had given me an okay, I could go back to work.
Yeah. Well, Cootie, yeah. I guess that was in '72, I guess, or like the end of '72.
When they went to Europe.
Or -- but you didn't join them over there.
No. When they came back.
When they came back. Well, Cootie, what you're really saying is when he himself was sick.
No. He wasn't sick then. I don't think so.
Well, he came back in November.
Yeah.
You know. And he went into hospital in January. So maybe we're talking about the year before.
Maybe the year before, when I taken sick.
Yeah.
When he went to Europe.

Yeah. But he probably came -- he probably went to Europe twice in there. Anyway, in other words, after you went back with him, you stayed in the band there while he was still alive, you stayed there about a year or more, didn't you?
I stayed in the band.
Huh? Yeah. You stayed in the band. Yeah.
Yes.
Well, listen, just one other thing I wanted to ask you about that. About Arthur Logan. What an awful blow for everybody.
Yeah.
Huh?
Yeah. It really was an awful blow.
A terrible thing for Duke.
Oh, yeah.
And him ill, and -- Cootie, did you figure that Duke was starting to feel poorly?
Oh, yeah.
Could you tell?

Yeah. That last trip we was on. See, he was working night by night. And I know he was sick. He was just barely making it. He told Mercer don't take the bus too far away from him, because he may have to leave any minute, to come home. That's when he left to come home.
Yeah.
And he brought the bus on back.
Yeah. Did you talk to him while he was in hospital?
No. I didn't get a chance to go up there. They didn't want any visitors. I used to send a message by Mercer.
No. I just wondered maybe if you talked to him on the phone or anything.
No. I didn't want to disturb him.
No.
I used to tell Mercer to tell him I'm saying a prayer for him every day.
Yeah. Yeah. And of course Harry was in hospital at that time, because Harry got pneumonia. Remember?
Harry got sick?
Well, Harry got sick while Duke was in the hospital. He had pneumonia.
Harry got sick before Duke.
Yeah. But then he came -- then he got better.
Then he got better.
Then he got better, but he was in the hospital then, you know with pneumonia. Because I know Duke called him to see if he was all right.
Uh-huh.
Well, that takes us to the funeral, which was a very beautiful thing. Don't you think it was?
Yeah. It was a very beautiful funeral. It brought me back to the time we played the concert there.
Yes. Yes.
The funeral did.
Yes. It sure did. It sure did. And at the very end, when they put the recording on, and up comes Alice's voice, and then Johnny --
Yeah.
-- I mean, that was -- that was like that was from up above or something, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Well, I know that -- I'm sure your feeling
is that he was the greatest musician and the greatest guy that you were ever around. I'm not putting words in your mouth, am I?
No, you're not. No, no. He was the greatest guy I ever met in life. Musician and man.
Yeah.
He really was. I never met a greater man than him.
No. No. Well, Cootie, then that was out of -- out of regard for him, I'm sure, too, that you didn't want to let Mercer down.
Oh, no.
You went out with Mercer, almost right away, didn't you?
Yeah. I went out with the band for that reason, the main reason, on account of Duke. Because I thought he needed me, and he really needed me at that time.
Yeah.

So I went on, and I think we had an interview at Johnson Publishers in Chicago. And I said -- they interviewed me -- I said the only reason I was here was on account of Duke Ellington. I had retired, and he called me and told me to come on back. I didn't have to play. Just to sit there. He missed looking at me, seeing me. And I said that's the main reason why I came back to the band. Because I
had retired and stopped blowing. I said, since he passed away, I think that Mercer needed me more than ever, so that's the reason why I'm with the band.
That's wonderful. That's wonderful. I think that's a good note for us to end this interview on. Don't you, Cootie?
Yeah. Wonderful. Thank you.
Thank you.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.title: Opening: copyright notice and start of the Smithsonian interview
segments.summary: Archive notice and title page; Helen Oakley Dance opens the May 1976 Smithsonian interview with Cootie Williams.

segments.title: Birth in Mobile, brothers and mother's music
segments.summary: Born 10 July 1911 in Mobile, third of four boys; mother played organ and piano and made them all study music; Cootie started on drums at five or six.

segments.title: Mother's death and the aunt who raised the boys
segments.summary: His mother died in childbirth with twins when he was seven or eight; an aunt raised the four brothers.

segments.title: Father's work: furs, then a gambling place on Davis Avenue
segments.summary: His father bought furs from country trappers, then opened a successful gambling place on Mobile's main street, forbidding Cootie to go near it.

segments.title: Father loses everything at the New Orleans race track
segments.summary: His father started going to New Orleans races and lost the home and gambling place; Cootie refused to return from New York when asked.

segments.title: Father as strike breaker in Houston, shot, then becomes a minister
segments.summary: His father moved to Houston as a strike breaker, was shot, was visited in hospital by Cootie, and afterwards turned to preaching.

segments.title: Father stays with Cootie in New York and then asks for money
segments.summary: His father stayed in New York, disapproved of Cootie's drinking and company, moved to the youngest brother, got $300 to go to California and died in the 1950s.

segments.title: Mother's character and what Cootie inherited
segments.summary: Cootie says he was between his religious, gentle mother and his father in character; he never got a whupping from her.

segments.title: Afraid of his father's whippings
segments.summary: Cootie was the only one of the brothers afraid of their father's whippings and so was careful to behave.

segments.title: The brothers, and the parents' marriage
segments.summary: He was close to the youngest and the next-older brother; the eldest helped raise them; his mother had a hard time with his father.

segments.title: Mobile as a wide-open seaport town
segments.summary: Mother's big Alabama family; Mobile was wide open, with a red light district Cootie saw delivering papers, and he knew nothing of drugs.

segments.title: Excelsior Brass Band and teacher Charlie Lipscomb
segments.summary: He remembers no country blues singers, only the Excelsior Brass Band in which his teacher Charlie Lipscomb played, the man who forbade jazz.

segments.title: Switching from drums to trumpet in the school band
segments.summary: Fooling with instruments in school band rehearsal he played Twelfth Street Rag on a trumpet; the bandmaster made him take it up and his father put him with Lipscomb.

segments.title: Working for Lipscomb in his pressing club and getting lessons
segments.summary: He delivered clothes by bicycle for $4 a week and a lesson, tried to copy Louis Armstrong records instead of practising, and got rapped on the head until he learned his lessons.

segments.title: Lipscomb's strict training: Arban, tone, reading
segments.summary: Lipscomb was a terrific trumpeter who taught breathing and reading from the Arban book, ignoring Cootie's jazz on the side.

segments.title: How the schooling got him the Fletcher Henderson job
segments.summary: His reading and phrasing training let him play first trumpet with Fletcher Henderson with no rehearsal when Pop Smith quit.

segments.title: Phonograph records and Louis Armstrong as idol
segments.summary: His father bought a phonograph; Cootie listened only to Louis Armstrong, learned the records by heart, and says Louis was his idol.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Bands from New Orleans advertising dances on trucks
segments.summary: Dance bands from New Orleans came to Mobile and played from trucks; the boy was allowed to play with them and learned the tunes.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Sitting in with the Pensacola Jazz Band and Edmond Hall
segments.summary: At about sixteen he sat in with Edmond Hall in the Pensacola Jazz Band, a Dixieland group playing by ear, when they visited Mobile.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Joining Eagle Eye Shields in Jacksonville
segments.summary: Edmond Hall went to pianist-leader Eagle Eye Shields, recommended Cootie, and his father arranged for his Jacksonville partner to look after him.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: The father's partner in Jacksonville, killed for passing as white
segments.summary: The gambler partner passed for white to play big games, was found out and shot on his front porch while Cootie lived with him.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Staying with Eagle Eye, then Alonzo Ross with Edmond Hall
segments.summary: Cootie stayed with Eagle Eye for a while before moving with Hall to Alonzo Ross's band.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: The carnival summer with Lester Young's family band
segments.summary: At about ten to twelve he heard Lester Young at a carnival, and his father let him join the Young family band; his brother went along.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Lipscomb cured him of nerves
segments.summary: His teacher hit him if he got nervous, and Cootie says he was never nervous in his career.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Lester Young and his father
segments.summary: Cootie does not think Lester's father was hard; Lester had offers from white bands but his father would not let him go.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Lester Young's different sound and what Cootie learned
segments.summary: Even then Lester was unlike Hawkins and unlike anyone Cootie had heard; Cootie learned some syncopations from him.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Life on the carnival: Lee, Irma and the father's pay
segments.summary: He ran with Lee and Irma rather than Lester, and was paid only fed meals and an occasional fifty cents.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Coming home, his brother hoboing, and the suit in East St. Louis
segments.summary: After a summer the brothers were sent money for the trip home; his brother hoboed, and Cootie bought his first long pants in East St. Louis.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Playing in the pit band for the carnival show
segments.summary: The band played for the stage acts and backed the Young family saxophone act, with Cootie reading the parts.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Mr. Young's talent and how his father understood him
segments.summary: Lester's father had a legitimate tone and liked Cootie's playing; Cootie's father understood he wanted nothing but the trumpet.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Practising all the time and his strict father
segments.summary: He blew the trumpet constantly, his father locked it away Sundays, took him to dances and made him be home before midnight.

segments.chapter: First bands and the road in the South
segments.title: Alonzo Ross's band at the Della Robia in Miami
segments.summary: Alonzo Ross's twelve-piece band played a colored nightclub in Miami with Hall and Fulbright, and broadcast from a Miami Beach station.

segments.title: Hired for the Rosemont Ballroom and the trip to New York
segments.summary: The owner of the Rosemont Ballroom in Brooklyn heard the radio broadcasts and hired the band; they came north by boat from Georgia.

segments.title: Staying behind in New York when the cooperative band went home
segments.summary: Cootie and Edmond Hall refused to go back to Florida, and lived on dime rolls and coffee from a Brooklyn baker.

segments.title: Trumpet night at the Bandbox and Chick Webb takes him in
segments.summary: Told to try the Bandbox jam sessions, he played trumpet night, and Chick Webb came, paid his landlady and took him in.

segments.title: Living with Chick Webb and Trueheart
segments.summary: Chick Webb took him under his wing, in rooms across from the Bandbox shared with guitarist Trueheart.

segments.title: Bandbox free breakfasts, Edmond Hall and the $35 scale
segments.summary: Musicians got free breakfast at the Bandbox run by Major; Hall landed a job with Claude Hopkins; Cootie earned $35 a week with Chick.

segments.title: Personnel of Chick Webb's band
segments.summary: Cootie tries to recall the early Chick Webb personnel with Dance.

segments.title: Chick Webb as drummer and leader
segments.summary: Chick had a very good ear, knew what he wanted, rehearsed the band and was serious about music.

segments.title: Union card problem keeps him from working with Chick
segments.summary: As a Mobile union member with no New York card he was barred from working with Chick Webb, though free to work with others.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson stand-in, the Roseland matinee and Big Green
segments.summary: Cootie went on the road with Fletcher Henderson, missed the Roseland matinee believing the stand-in was over, and Bobby Stark protected him from Big Green.

segments.title: A year with Fletcher Henderson: Hawkins, Bobby Stark, and the arrangements
segments.summary: In the Henderson band he was most moved by Bobby Stark, heard Hawkins and Benny Carter battle, and thought the arrangements terrific.

segments.title: Johnny Hodges tells Duke about Cootie
segments.summary: Johnny Hodges, once with Chick Webb, recommended Cootie to Duke after Bubber Miley was fired; Cootie had thought the Ellington band comedy music.

segments.title: Joining Duke and learning the plunger from Tricky Sam
segments.summary: Hired to play Bubber Miley's plunger role, he had never used one and learned it by listening to Tricky Sam Nanton.

segments.title: Why Duke fired Bubber Miley, and Duke's hands-off style
segments.summary: Bubber was the only man Duke fired, for being absent when big shots came; Duke never told Cootie what to play.

segments.title: Ellington band members: Tricky, Freddy Jenkins, Arthur Whetsel, Posey
segments.summary: Dance and Cootie recall his friends and the trumpet section of the early band, and Tricky Sam.

segments.title: Toby, Johnny Hodges and Barney Bigard
segments.summary: Cootie got along with Hodges, called Bigard a different type but friendly; the band was like a family.

segments.title: Harry Carney and Sonny Greer
segments.summary: Carney joined 1927, Hodges 1928, Cootie 1929; Cootie says Sonny Greer fit the band as no one else could, and liked Louis Bellson.

segments.title: Chick Webb personnel recalled
segments.summary: Dance reads out the Chick Webb personnel found in the interval.

segments.title: First record session, as Jabbo Smith's replacement
segments.summary: He was told to stand in on the James P. Johnson record for the missing Jabbo Smith, and was introduced to the studio as Jabbo.

segments.title: The Cotton Club shows bored him
segments.summary: He found rehearsing the Cotton Club shows tedious, though the band played plenty behind acts such as the Berry Brothers.

segments.title: Cotton Club gangsters and segregation
segments.summary: The club was segregated and run by Owney Madden and Herman Stark; Cootie remembers little.

segments.title: Jabbo Smith and his lost promise
segments.summary: Cootie admires Jabbo's playing in 1928 and regrets that he dropped out of sight in Milwaukee.

segments.title: Mills office, pay on the road, and the Cotton Club as home base
segments.summary: Pay came from the road manager, and the band always returned to the Cotton Club between tours.

segments.title: Marriage to Catherine and other band weddings
segments.summary: Cootie married Catherine after joining Duke; they discuss when Hodges and Chick Webb married.

segments.title: The Amos and Andy film in Hollywood
segments.summary: Making the Amos and Andy picture was exciting for a band that was among the first to appear in film.

segments.title: The voyage to England, poker and not drinking
segments.summary: On the crossing the band played poker all night while Duke drank brandy and champagne; Cootie did not drink until he had his band.

segments.title: English fans who knew every record
segments.summary: In England fans had all their records and knew all the details, while American audiences did not.

segments.title: Jazz audiences in Europe versus America
segments.summary: Cootie says Europe is educated about jazz and America is not, blaming disc jockeys; jazz courses only started seven years earlier.

segments.title: The first concert, at the London Palladium
segments.summary: Dance recalls the band's first concert-hall performance; Cootie recalls playing theaters as an act and enjoys audiences who understand jazz.

segments.title: The royal party and the Prince on Sonny's drums
segments.summary: At a millionaire's party a royal prince played Sonny Greer's drums, and the band was received warmly.

segments.title: Duke adds men to the band
segments.summary: They try to recall when Tizol and Lawrence Brown joined, the first expansions, and when Ben Webster arrived.

segments.title: Ivy Anderson joins the act
segments.summary: Ivy came with the band as a lively entertainer; the act was well rehearsed, and she played poker with the band on trains.

segments.title: Pause, and resumption of the interview on May 13th
segments.summary: Tape pause; the interview resumes on May 13th with the question of the early days of the band.

segments.title: Everyone chipped in on songs for $25
segments.summary: In the early band members contributed to songs and sold them to Duke for $25; Bigard later sued over Mood Indigo, but Cootie did not.

segments.title: Writing Concerto for Cootie and Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me
segments.summary: Cootie composed Concerto for Cootie alone and begged Duke to buy it on a bus from Boston for $25; the song later became a hit.

segments.title: Other Ellington compositions and Billy Strayhorn writing for Johnny Hodges
segments.summary: Who wrote on Sophisticated Lady and other numbers; Strayhorn wrote for Johnny Hodges when Cootie was there.

segments.title: First Ellington sessions, 1930
segments.summary: Dance lists the 1930 sessions: Rent Party Blues, Jungle Blues, Ring Dem Bells, The Mooch, where Cootie used the plunger.

segments.title: Two styles: plunger and open horn
segments.summary: The plunger was Bubber Miley's trademark that Cootie learned from Tricky Sam; his own open style came from Louis Armstrong.

segments.title: Advice to young players: listen to everyone
segments.summary: Cootie advises youngsters to listen to all good jazz players rather than one, so they find their own voice.

segments.title: Playing solos: Fletcher's first chair versus Duke
segments.summary: Before Duke he played only lead parts with Fletcher; he always practised jazz at home as a student.

segments.title: Telling a story with a solo
segments.summary: Cootie describes shaping a solo like telling a story, with a statement, a release, and a built second chorus.

segments.title: Playing off the melody, not the chords
segments.summary: He needs a melody to improvise on, and says his generation played off melody; chord-based playing came later.

segments.title: How Duke wrote for individuals and built records in the studio
segments.summary: Duke gave each player parts that fit them, and record numbers grew from a theme and solos.

segments.title: East St. Louis Toodle-oo as theme
segments.summary: On the 1930 session Cootie played plunger on the Ellington theme song East St. Louis; they note A Train replaced it.

segments.title: Rockin' in Rhythm and Harry James's Pecking
segments.summary: Cootie's solo on Rockin' in Rhythm was taken by Harry James as a song he got no credit for; Rockin' in Rhythm came out of Pigmeat Markham rehearsal.

segments.title: Creole Rhapsody session
segments.summary: Cootie cannot remember Creole Rhapsody well.

segments.title: It Don't Mean a Thing and the title's origin
segments.summary: Cootie says he used to tell Duke 'it don't mean a thing if it ain't got that swing', which became the 1932 title.

segments.title: Ivy Anderson's personality on stage
segments.summary: Cootie says Ivy was better in person than on records; Dance discusses her Oriental Theater debut and Duke's liking for singers.

segments.title: Black and Tan Fantasy, Creole Love Call and the film
segments.summary: Dance lists Cootie's jungle-style features such as Black and Tan and Creole Love Call, and the short film.

segments.title: The band grows and starts playing theaters
segments.summary: By 1931-32 the band was growing into sections and began playing theaters; there were three trumpets.

segments.title: Arthur Whetsel, Freddy Jenkins and the trumpet section
segments.summary: Artie had a beautiful tone but little power; Duke switched parts around; Freddy Jenkins was a peculiar stylist and good section man.

segments.title: Blending in a section, and the early unified trumpet section
segments.summary: Blending means staying under the lead; only the earliest trumpet section tried to be one man.

segments.title: Section leaders and the quarrels of later years
segments.summary: As changes came, players resented being told anything, and arguments arose when Cat Anderson was supposed to lead.

segments.title: New men left to find their parts
segments.summary: New saxophone players had no one to show them the unwritten parts and sat lost until Harry Carney or others helped; Ben Webster was liked.

segments.title: Parts given out orally on record dates; no written bass part
segments.summary: On sessions Duke dictated notes at the piano; he never wrote a bass part until later years.

segments.title: Bassists: Wellman Braud and Billy Taylor
segments.summary: Braud was a New Orleans bass player who did not read; Cootie thought Billy Taylor the best band bassist, who then dropped out of sight.

segments.title: Walking home with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: Cootie, living at Braud's house, walked home with Louis Armstrong from the Savoy after his Cotton Club job, one of his biggest thrills.

segments.title: Following Louis wherever he played
segments.summary: Cootie went to hear Louis whenever he could and was interested in no one else; he says Louis played best with Les Hite's band.

segments.title: Los Angeles: hearing Louis at Sebastian's and miniature golf
segments.summary: On the West Coast the band heard Louis in person and ran in from the miniature golf course to catch him on the radio.

segments.title: Duke's stage presentation and conducting
segments.summary: Duke could not remember names when introducing singers early on and seldom conducted before extended works.

segments.title: Duke's hands-off management and never firing anyone
segments.summary: Duke gave men freedom, never bothered anyone and fired no one, even when Paul Gonsalves or Willie could have been.

segments.title: Reminiscing in Tempo and Duke always looking forward
segments.summary: Duke wrote every day and never looked back; his biggest hits came from the original band when men chipped in.

segments.title: Mood Indigo, Solitude and Duke's own numbers
segments.summary: Mood Indigo was part Duke and part Bigard; Dance discusses Solitude and numbers like Prelude to a Kiss that are all Duke.

segments.title: Strayhorn's work habits compared with Duke's
segments.summary: Duke wrote continually; Strayhorn wrote only on assignment and liked to party and jam.

segments.title: Duke as accompanist
segments.summary: Cootie played better with Duke than any pianist, because Duke felt every move and left nothing open.

segments.title: Strayhorn joining the band and writing for Johnny Hodges
segments.summary: Strayhorn was respected once they played his music; his only band number was A Train, the rest written with and for Hodges.

segments.title: Mercer Ellington and Johnny Hodges' own band
segments.summary: Dance and Cootie sort out Mercer's credits and Hodges leaving to lead a band with Strayhorn.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: Duke arranged Cootie's departure to Goodman
segments.summary: When Goodman approached him Cootie told Duke, who set up the deal and later told him he was too big to come back.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: The Ellington band after Cootie and Johnny left
segments.summary: They discuss the 1940 band, the last session Concerto for Cootie, Ben Webster and who left next.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: How Benny Goodman hired him
segments.summary: Goodman approached Cootie through his brother Irving; he liked the band's beat, and the pay was settled in New York.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: The Goodman sextet year
segments.summary: Duke advised him to be featured only with the sextet; it was the most relaxed and best-paid year of his career.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: Goodman's discipline and the big band
segments.summary: Goodman rehearsed the band hard and everyone did as told; Cootie was used to discipline from Ellington.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: What he learned from Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Benny and Duke were different men; Cootie learned handling and rehearsing a band, though he could not pay for rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
segments.title: Buddies in the Goodman band
segments.summary: His friends in the band were Irving Goodman, Charlie Christian, Mike Bryant and Georgie Auld.

segments.title: Leaving Goodman and starting a big band
segments.summary: He left when his year was up, started a band at the Grand Terrace in Chicago, and lost money at first.

segments.title: Agencies and the fifty percent cut
segments.summary: Booking agencies demanded fifty percent of the band; he refused at first with the William Morris Agency but then went with Moe Gale.

segments.title: Hits and refusing to pay Moe Gale fifty percent
segments.summary: Cherry Red Blues and Things Ain't What They Used to Be made him successful; he stopped paying fifty percent and bookings dropped.

segments.title: Buddy Johnson and the white field
segments.summary: They discuss why bands like Buddy Johnson's, strong only in the black market, never broke through.

segments.title: Changing agencies and the Savoy house band
segments.summary: He changed agencies, bookings fell, and he got the Savoy house band, which was cut to seven pieces.

segments.title: The seven-piece Savoy group
segments.summary: He lists the seven-piece group, with organ, Rupert Cole and Les Jenkins, and tries to remember the tenor player.

segments.title: Going to Texas for a tenor player
segments.summary: With John Hammond's help he went to Texas to hire a tenor player but instead found Eddie Cleanhead Vinson singing blues.

segments.title: Finding and rehearsing Eddie Cleanhead Vinson
segments.summary: Cootie brought Vinson to New York, got him a proper horn and case, and coaxed him through his first rehearsal.

segments.title: First band personnel: Joe Guy and Louis Bacon
segments.summary: Dance and Cootie sort through the 1942 band including trumpeters Joe Guy and Louis Bacon.

segments.title: Why he hired modern players
segments.summary: Cootie liked modern jazz players who were breaking new ground, including Bud Powell and Charlie Parker.

segments.title: Writing the verse to Monk's 'Round Midnight
segments.summary: Monk came around the band from Minton's, and Cootie wrote the verse to 'Round Midnight, which is only on his record.

segments.title: Hiring good trumpet players and hating bad musicians
segments.summary: He wants all good players to play, but says a bad musician sitting next to him is his enemy as he cannot fire him.

segments.title: Policing the Ellington band when Duke would not
segments.summary: In Duke's band Cootie hollered at Hodges and Bigard if they played wrong or fooled around, since Duke never spoke.

segments.title: Sonny Greer's drinking and why Cootie wanted to leave
segments.summary: Cootie got angry at Sonny's drinking and falling off the drums, one reason he wanted to leave.

segments.title: Tolerating Bud Powell and Charlie Parker half high
segments.summary: As a leader he tolerated great players like Bud Powell who came in half high.

segments.title: Charlie Parker in the band
segments.summary: Cootie calls Parker the most influential jazz musician; Parker left because Cootie only let him solo, not play parts.

segments.title: First hearing Parker with Jay McShann
segments.summary: Cootie first heard Charlie Parker with Jay McShann's band.

segments.title: Bud Powell, George Treadwell and Sarah Vaughan at the Apollo
segments.summary: Parker's friends in the band included Bud Powell and George Treadwell, who met Sarah Vaughan on Amateur Night at the Apollo.

segments.title: Bud Powell's breakdown in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Bud came in late and wild at a Philadelphia date, was beaten by police and hospitalised in Bellevue, and never returned.

segments.title: Mixing modern and older players
segments.summary: Cootie believed in blending modern players with older ones before Ellington did.

segments.title: Charlie Holmes, Sam Taylor and Bob Dorsey
segments.summary: Cootie's saxophones included Charlie Holmes, Bob Dorsey and Sam The Man Taylor, who got few solos.

segments.title: Hiring and training Pearl Bailey
segments.summary: He hired Pearl after hearing her at a rehearsal for her different voice, and pushed her to do it his way.

segments.title: Kenny Kersey and Illinois Jacquet
segments.summary: Dance and Cootie recall Kenny Kersey, a boogie-woogie pianist, who went with Andy Kirk.

segments.title: Hiring Lockjaw Davis and teaching young players
segments.summary: He heard Lockjaw jamming at Minton's, took time to teach talent to read, and says he learned from Goodman.

segments.title: Searching for Emmett Berry and Money Johnson
segments.summary: Cootie cannot place Emmett Berry or Money Johnson in his band.

segments.title: Starting to drink after forming his own band
segments.summary: Cootie began drinking some two years after forming his band, drinking and then laying off, and quit entirely in the late 1950s.

segments.title: Building arrangements around the leader
segments.summary: Arrangements were built around Cootie's trumpet, and he and Dance discuss a leader's duty to deliver.

segments.title: The Savoy years and Charlie Buchanan
segments.summary: From 1955 to 1962 he led seven pieces at the Savoy, hired by manager Charlie Buchanan, who kept him because he played all the dance nights.

segments.title: Savoy small-group personnel and the organ
segments.summary: He recalls organist Fabulous Preston and Rupert Cole, and how three horns plus organ sounded like a big band.

segments.title: Arrangers and singers for his bands
segments.summary: Don Redman wrote for Pearl Bailey, others for Vinson; ballads went to a white arranger; later a country blues guitarist sang.

segments.title: Not singing, and doing a single after the Savoy closed
segments.summary: He did not sing with his own band; on a single in Toronto audiences wanted him to sing and sit in with bad pickup groups.

segments.title: Harold Baker, Willie Cook and Clark Terry
segments.summary: Cootie praises Harold Baker, Willie Cook and Clark Terry, who he thought did not get a chance with Duke.

segments.title: Paul Gonsalves and Duke's tactics
segments.summary: Paul was great when straight; Duke called Paul's hardest number when he was stoned or sleeping and used Harold Ashby as a replacement.

segments.title: Drummers, trombonists and bassists
segments.summary: Short opinions on Rufus Jones, Booty Wood, Jimmy Blanton and Gus Johnson.

segments.title: A road tour with Benny Goodman in 1962
segments.summary: Before rejoining Duke he made a road tour with Goodman after Goodman returned from Russia.

segments.title: Rejoining Duke's band after twenty-three years
segments.summary: He told Harry Carney he was ready and found it felt like being back home.

segments.title: Afro Bossa Salsa, Tootie for Cootie and the New Orleans Suite
segments.summary: Dance recalls Cootie's records and pieces Duke wrote for him after his return.

segments.title: Ellington's works and tours from 1963: My People, Near East, Far East
segments.summary: Dance prompts the 1963-64 tours and the Far East Suite.

segments.title: Sacred Concerts and Duke's religion; the number written for Cootie
segments.summary: Duke read the Bible many times; he wrote a Sacred Concert piece for Cootie after trying it out on piano.

segments.title: Strayhorn's death and Duke giving credit
segments.summary: Strayhorn died in 1967 after sending Blood Count; Cootie agrees Duke always gave Billy credit.

segments.title: Alice Babbs and the Second Sacred Concert
segments.summary: Cootie praises Alice Babbs, for whom Duke wrote, as another Ellington voice.

segments.title: The 1968 South America tour and the 1969 White House party
segments.summary: The band was mobbed in South America and Wild Bill joined in 1969.

segments.title: Johnny Hodges' death and his relationship with Duke
segments.summary: Hodges' death in 1970 was a blow; Cootie says he and Duke were very close.

segments.title: Cootie's 1973 lung illness
segments.summary: Taken ill after playing A Train, Cootie was sent home by Dr. Arthur Logan, hospitalised, and told to rest a year.

segments.title: Duke asks him to come back
segments.summary: Duke called twice asking him to return, saying he only had to sit there; Cootie went back for him alone.

segments.title: Dr. Logan's death and Duke's last illness
segments.summary: Dr. Arthur Logan's death was a blow; Duke was sick on his last trip and Cootie sent prayers via Mercer.

segments.title: Duke's funeral and why Cootie stayed with Mercer
segments.summary: The funeral recalled the Sacred Concert; Cootie calls Duke the greatest man he met and stayed on to help Mercer.
